[{"page": 102, "text": "The absence of the cumulative training effect from the snatch and half squat with the 
barbell on the shoulders to the competitive event in the men’s and women’s 400m 
hurdles, as well as the barbell snatch to the 200 and 400m can be interpreted in different 
ways.  In one case, it indicates the ineffectiveness of the given exercise, while in another, 
that the positive transfer is conditioned by the use of other methodological means.  This 
relates primarily to the number of repetitions in one set, the compactness of the strength 
training sessions or their parts, and likewise the zones of intensity used.   
 
It is obvious that the cumulative effect from strength exercises will appear only when 
they are close to the competitive event according to the biomechanical aspects and 
methodological parameters.   
85 "}, {"page": 103, "text": "Transfer of Physical Abilities in the Jumps When Using 
Different Exercises 
 
Considering the specifics of training in the track and field jumps, we studied the 
influence of different runs (sprints), jumps, throws and strength exercises that are most 
frequently used in sport practice and their relationship to the main movement (event). 
 
The system of training jumpers has been made more complex in the last 10 years 
considering the duration of the cycles of developing sports form during which a large 
number of specialized exercises are used together with repetition of the competitive event 
and its’ separate segments [42, 81,212].  The percentage of special exercises, in 
comparison to the total volume of training time, was 50-60%.  Improving the competitive 
event by repeating the entire movement comprised 20-30% of the total time.  A frequent 
exception to this were high jumpers whose total training loads in the competitive event 
training were 10-20% greater than athletes specializing in other jump events.  The percent 
of strength and throwing exercises varied between 15-25%. 
 
Now we will analyze the factual material touching on the problem of training transfer of 
different exercises to the competitive exercise.  We will begin with the men’s and 
women’s long jump.  The correlational analyses (tables 61,62) substantiate that the 
positive cumulative effect is observed when all types of run and jump exercises are used 
and the two throwing exercises—throwing the shot forward and backward are absent.  
The greatest interrelationships were seen in the jumps with a short approach run, in the 
30m run with a flying start and in the ten-fold jump from place.  In the barbell snatch 
with men, a positive training transfer was observed when the sports results were from 
6.5-7.3m and in women from 5.0-6.1m.  Several others were seen in the half squat with 
the barbell on the shoulder.  In the women, the cumulative effect appeared on all levels of 
sports results and in the men only on three, from 6.5-7.6m. 
 
 
 
86 "}]

jumps (vertical jump, long jump, and triple jump from place) and multiple jumps (five-
and ten-fold) then it can be seen that the second form of exercises (multiple jumps) have 
a greater number of cases in which the correlation is higher than with the first exercises.

yearly cycle, the athletes use a sufficiently large number of exercises repeating the basic

different weights.  The deviation range when using lighter and heavier implements in 
comparison to the competitive implement weight, can vary from several percent to the 
tens and even hundreds of percent.   
 
It is generally known that for developing strength abilities, heavier implements are used 
and for speed, lighter.  In the last two decades the total training loads used in the year-
round training cycle with the use of lighter, heavier and competitive weight implements 
varied between 30-50% of the total amount of time used for training.   
 
In the last 50-60 years in the past century, athletes basically used the competitive weight 
implement.  Heavier and lighter implements were used sporadically and in small volume.

competition.  Usually the heavier and lighter implements were used during 4-6 week

[{"page": 115, "text": "presence of a positive correlational interrelationship between lighter, heavier and 
competitive weight implements in the structure of the entire movement in all types of 
throws, on different levels of sports mastery.  The greatest amounts of correlational 
interrelationships were most frequently found in cases where the deviations between the 
lighter and heavier implement weights was insignificant in relation to the competitive---
from 10-20%.  The smallest correlation was fixed in the hammer throw when athletes had 
results in the at 60-65m range when throwing the 16kg weight (0.425).  A weak 
interrelationship (0.365) was observed between results in the shotput with weights of 5.0 
and 7.260 kg in athletes throwing the shot 20-21m. 
 
The compiled data once again substantiated the correctness of the position in the theory 
and practice of track and field, that throws with lighter and heavier implements appear to 
be the most transferable to the competitive exercise.  The reason for this is that they are 
identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical 
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the 
muscular groups in the execution, the muscle work regimes and so on.   
 
What is pertinent here is that those negative consequences, which always have a place 
here, are so insignificant that after ceasing use of one or another lighter or heavier 
implement, they can be eliminated in several weekly cycles.  The latter of these (heavier 
implements) relates to the deviations in technical mastery which has been noted by 
several authors [18, 152].  Foremost among these is the change in the release angle of the 
implement during the final effort, the deviation or lean of the trunk backward, the 
decreased amplitude of movement of the implement and so on.   
 
In practically all track and field disciplines, there are no identical actions, according to all 
parameters of the exercise, that repeat those in the competitive event.  Because of this, 
when using one or another exercise, it is necessary to a large measure, to think of its 
positive effects, not about its negatives.  The exercises should be selected so that the 
positive influence prevails.

[{"page": 115, "text": "presence of a positive correlational interrelationship between lighter, heavier and 
competitive weight implements in the structure of the entire movement in all types of 
throws, on different levels of sports mastery.  The greatest amounts of correlational 
interrelationships were most frequently found in cases where the deviations between the 
lighter and heavier implement weights was insignificant in relation to the competitive---
from 10-20%.  The smallest correlation was fixed in the hammer throw when athletes had 
results in the at 60-65m range when throwing the 16kg weight (0.425).  A weak 
interrelationship (0.365) was observed between results in the shotput with weights of 5.0 
and 7.260 kg in athletes throwing the shot 20-21m. 
 
The compiled data once again substantiated the correctness of the position in the theory 
and practice of track and field, that throws with lighter and heavier implements appear to 
be the most transferable to the competitive exercise.  The reason for this is that they are 
identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical 
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the 
muscular groups in the execution, the muscle work regimes and so on.   
 
What is pertinent here is that those negative consequences, which always have a place 
here, are so insignificant that after ceasing use of one or another lighter or heavier 
implement, they can be eliminated in several weekly cycles.  The latter of these (heavier 
implements) relates to the deviations in technical mastery which has been noted by 
several authors [18, 152].  Foremost among these is the change in the release angle of the 
implement during the final effort, the deviation or lean of the trunk backward, the 
decreased amplitude of movement of the implement and so on.   
 
In practically all track and field disciplines, there are no identical actions, according to all 
parameters of the exercise, that repeat those in the competitive event.  Because of this, 
when using one or another exercise, it is necessary to a large measure, to think of its 
positive effects, not about its negatives.  The exercises should be selected so that the 
positive influence prevails.

[{"page": 143, "text": "Transfer of Physical Abilities When Using Different 
Exercises in Cyclical Events Requiring the Display of 
Endurance 
 
An increase in sports achievement in the cyclical events that require the display of 
endurance, is conditioned by the presence of a high level of development of the anaerobic 
and aerobic abilities and the corresponding body systems.  For their improvement, a large 
number of different exercises is used.  The exercises are different from one another first 
of all by the duration of the training effect---the distance of the segments used.  For 
development of the alactate anaerobic abilities short segments are used---anywhere from 
10-30 up to 150m so that the duration of work does not go above 20sec and the intensity 
of the work overcome is maximal.   
 
The lactate anaerobic abilities are developed when using longer distances from 150-400m 
and the time of covering these distances varies between 30-60 sec and the intensity of the 
training work is in the zone of 90-95% of maximum.  For simultaneous improvement of 
the lactate anaerobic and aerobic abilities, training loads that last anywhere from 1-5min 
with the intensity at 80-95% of maximum are used.  This can take the form of segments 
that are over 400m long up to several kilometers [154, 183, 215, 216]. 
 
Long segments are used most frequently to improve aerobic abilities.  The segments used 
depend upon the specialty of the athletes and their level of mastery.  Depending on the 
level of mastery, segments can be up to 10-30km or identical loads that can be fulfilled 
over the duration of several hours using a low zone intensity [154, 183, 215, 216]. 
 
We should also note that in the process of developing anaerobic capabilities, the duration 
of the training segments, the use of intensity zones as well as the distances and character 
of the rest between separate segments or series, are taken into consideration.  We will 
now look at the segments (distances) that are used most frequently in the training of 
athletes specializing in different events requiring the display of endurance. 
126 "}, {"page": 144, "text": " 
We will begin with middle distance runners.  They use segments anywhere from 60-
100m up to 10-15km in length.  Runners specializing in the steeplechase (3,000m with 
hurdles) 5,000m and 10,000m (both men and women) as well as women specializing in 
the 3,000m run, use distances from 100m to 20-30km.  Marathoners use distances from 
400m – to several 10s of kilometers.  Also used are training loads lasting more than 2hrs.   
 
In sports walking, running as well as walking are used for short and long distances.  For 
women specializing in the 10km walk, the distances vary from 1-20km, and for 20 and 
50km men walkers—from  1-30km.  The latter as well as marathoners, do training work 
lasting more than 2hrs.   
 
After competition a general picture of the means and methods of developing anaerobic 
and aerobic abilities used in cyclical sports that require endurance is revealed.  In general 
terms, we will present experimental material which shows the range of transfer of the 
physical abilities in the middle, long and super long running distances as well as in sports 
walking for the 10 (women), and 20 and 50km (men) events. 
 
In the men’s and women’s 800m run, there is a range of transfer of physical abilities 
beginning with the 60m run from a low start and ending with the 5000m run (tables 89, 
97).  The latter distances with the men, had a place on two levels of sports mastery 
(1:56:00-2:00:00 and 1:52:00 1:56:00) and with the women, on one level (2:15:00-
2:20:00).  The greatest amounts of correlational interrelationship were fixed in the 400, 
600, and 1000m runs.  In performers of both sexes, the correlation varied from 0.700-
0.900.  In men, the biggest transfer was with the 1000m run (0.912, 0.876, 0.905, 0.856).  
A sharp decrease in the amount of correlational interrelationship was observed in the 
1500m run in men and women.  A weak interrelationship was seen with the 3000 and 
500m runs. 
 
The range of transfer of physical abilities in the men’s 1500m run begins with the 60m 
segment and ends with the 5000m distance.  The cumulative effect has a place on all 
127 "}, {"page": 145, "text": "levels of sports mastery.  In women, as in the men, the range of transfer begins with the 
60m but ends on the 10,000m distance.  In the latter case it appears on three of the five 
levels of sports mastery.  The greatest amount of correlational interrelationship is 
observed in participants of both sexes in the 800, 1000 and 3000m runs (table 90, 98).   
 
Results of the correlational analysis of 800 and 1500m runners shows that with an 
increase in the competitive distance, the range of transfer of physical abilities increases.  
Thus, for men participants in the “long sprint” (800m) transfer is seen with the 5000m 
distance, and in the women specializing in the 1500m run, transfer has a place in the 
10,000m distance.  In the 800m runners greatest transfer was seen with the 600 and 
1000m and with the 1500m runners, in the 800, 1000, and 3000m runs. 
 
In comparing the amounts of interrelationship between results in the competitive running 
distance with women specializing in the 800 and 1500m, we came to the conclusion that 
in the 800m runners, results in the 1500m run were more transferable to the competitive 
event (coefficient of correlation varied from 0.657-0.788), than in the 1500m runners 
(from 0.380-0.652).   
 
Analysis of the results of the ten strongest 800 and 1500m runners in the world 
throughout the history of track and field, shows that the world record holders in the 
1500m run frequently demonstrate a higher level of achievement in the 800m run than 
world record holders in the 800m run in the 1500m distance.  Only one athlete, S. Coe 
was able to have a world record in both distances. 
 
The range of transfer of physical abilities in steeplechase runners begins with the 600m 
run (three levels of sports mastery) and ends with the 10,000m run.  A positive transfer is 
not observed with results in the 100 and 400m runs.  The most transferable were the 
3,000 and 5,000m runs.  Here the coefficient of correlation in four instances was greater 
than 0.700 and in one---0.800 (table 91).  In the 600, 800, 1,000, 1,500 and 10,000m runs, 
the coefficient was very low (from 0.356-0.497), which signifies the weak 
interrelationship between the studied indices.  However, some of the strongest athletes 
128 "}, {"page": 146, "text": "show high sports results not only in the 5,000m distance but in the 1,500, 3,000, and 
10,000m.   Note that the leading runner, H. Rono, set the world record in the 5,000, 
10,000m and steeplechase in his time. 
 
In the women’s 3,000m the range of transfer of physical abilities is somewhat greater 
(table 99), than with the steeplechase runners.  Here it begins with the 400m run and ends 
with the 10,000m run.  The positive interrelationship had a place on all levels of the 
segments tested.  Most transfer was in the 1,000, 1,500, and 5,000m runs.  The 
coefficients of correlation varied from 0.725-0.906.  Transfer to the competitive event 
from the 100 and 200m runs were non-existent.  Practice substantiates that many of the 
strongest 3,000m women runners in the world (Olympic and world champions and record 
holders) showed the greatest results in the mixed distances.  Thus, the former world 
record holder in this distance, T. Kazankina, two time Olympic champion in the 1500m 
and one time winner in the 800m and American M. Decker who was world champion in 
the 1500 and 3000m runs.   
 
The range of transfer of physical abilities in the 5000m run, both in the men as in the 
women, begins with the 600m run (table 92, 100).  In men, transfer appears on all levels 
of sports mastery and in women, only on two (16.00-16.30 and 16.30-17.00min).  The 
cumulative effect is also seen in the marathon results. Here it is observed both in the men 
as in the women only on two levels of sports mastery.  The 800, 1000, 1500, 3000 
10,000m and half marathon, show a positive transfer taking place on all levels of sports 
mastery. The greatest transfer appears in the 3,000 and 10,000m run.  In men, the 
coefficient of correlation in these distances was somewhat higher than in the women.  
 
Results of the correlational analysis substantiates that the range of transfer of physical 
abilities in athletes specializing in the 10,000m run begins with results in the 600m run 
and ends with results in the marathon (table 93, 101).  The first distance has a place on 
two consecutive levels (28.00-28.30 and 28.30-29.00min), and the second, on all levels 
from 28.00-34.00min.  In the women, the range of transfer is somewhat less than in the 
men.  It begins with results in the 1,500m run.  However, runners of both sexes show that 
129 "}, {"page": 147, "text": "the greatest coefficient of correlation was in the 5,000m run as well as in the half 
marathon and marathon.  
 
Results of the last ten world record holders in the 5,000 and 10,000m is evidence of the 
fact that only one athlete was able to set a world record in both distances.  This is despite 
the fact that all runners in the 5000 and 10000m show high sports results and also 
frequently run both of these distances in the Olympic games (V. Kotz, L. Viren, M. Ifter 
and others).  It appears that the ten strongest runners in the world in the 5000m in all of 
track and field history, in most cases do not appear as the strongest top ten runners in the 
10,000m.  Here the discussion is of the ten best results shown by the athletes in the 
5,000m and 10,000m.  Also, the ten strongest runners in the 10,000m rarely enter into the 
top group of the strongest runners in the world in the 5,000m.  And here is still another 
interesting fact. In comparing the transfer (coefficients of correlation) results in the 
10,000m run to results in the 5000m run (tables 93, 101) and results in the 5,000m to 
results in the 10000m (tables 92, 100), it can be seen that in the first case, the coefficients 
of correlation are somewhat higher than in the second. 
 
The range of transfer of physical abilities in men marathoners begins with the 5000m run 
and in the women with the 3000m run (tables 94, 102).  In the men, the cumulative effect 
in the 5000m distance is observed on all levels of sports mastery and in the women, in the 
3000m run only on two beginning levels (2:55:00-3:05:00 and 3:05:00-3:15:00).  Most 
transfer was seen from the 10,000m run and the half marathon.  The coefficient of 
correlation for women as for the men, varied from 0.700-0.800 and more.   
 
Results of the strongest marathoners over the last five Olympic cycles is evidence of the 
fact that not one of the men was able to establish a world record in the 10,000m and be 
victorious in the marathon.  However, some of the strongest 10,000m runners in the 
world (K. Lopesh), by switching to the marathon became Olympic champion.  A 
somewhat different picture is seen with the women.  G. Waitz set a world record in the 
marathon four times, two times in the 3000m, one time each in cross country at the 15km, 
10 and 20mile distances, and likewise, in the half marathon.  Another outstanding 
130 "}, {"page": 148, "text": "woman, I. Christianson was world record holder in the marathon and also in the 5,000 
and 10,000m.  
 
As a rule, most of the strongest world marathon runners show high results in the 10,000m 
run.  This is explained first of all by the fact that almost all of them began by specializing 
in long distance running and only later, after the passage of time, went over to the 
marathon.  In bettering their sports results in the marathon they also improved their 
results in the 10,000m run.  But none of them set a record at this distance during this 
time.  Besides this, in most cases the time (year) of setting personal bests in both 
distances did not coincide. 
 
In athletes specializing in the 10km walk, the cumulative effect was fixed at two running 
distances (5,000 and 10,000m) and in the 1 and 5km walks (table 103).  The cumulative 
effect was absent only on one level of sports results (the 5,000m run).  In the running 
exercises the coefficient of correlation in all cases was very low---from 0.354 up to 0.387 
which shows the weak interrelationship between indices in the 5,000 and 10,000m run 
with the competitive event.  In the 1km walk, it varied on the level of 0.700-0.800.  In the 
5km walk, the coefficient of correlation in three cases exceeded 0.800 and in one, 0.700.   
 
The range of transfer of physical abilities in athletes specializing in the 20km walk begins 
with special developmental exercises and results in the 1km walk and ends with results in 
the 50km walk (table 95).  The cumulative effect also has a place in the 10,000m run.  
The biggest coefficients of correlation were fixed in the 10km walk and the smallest in 
the run at this distance—from  0.354-0.387.  In the 50km walkers, the transfer of physical 
abilities to the 1km walk is observed on two levels of sports mastery and in the 5, 10, and 
20km walks on all levels (table 96).  Most transfer was with the results in the 10 and 
20km walks.  A weak correlation of the interrelationship was observed with indices in the 
10,000m run. 
 
Results of the correlational analysis of athletes specializing in the 20 and 50km walks 
show that in the first group, results in the 10 and 50km have the greatest transfer while 
131 "}, {"page": 149, "text": "for the second group (50km) results in the 10 and 20km walks.  Almost the same was the

coefficient of correlation in all instances did not go above 0.400, which indicates the

over the duration of several hours using a low zone intensity [154, 183, 215, 216]. 
 
We should also note that in the process of developing anaerobic capabilities, the duration 
of the training segments, the use of intensity zones as well as the distances and character 
of the rest between separate segments or series, are taken into consideration.  We will 
now look at the segments (distances) that are used most frequently in the training of 
athletes specializing in different events requiring the display of endurance. 
126 "}, {"page": 144, "text": " 
We will begin with middle distance runners.  They use segments anywhere from 60-
100m up to 10-15km in length.  Runners specializing in the steeplechase (3,000m with 
hurdles) 5,000m and 10,000m (both men and women) as well as women specializing in 
the 3,000m run, use distances from 100m to 20-30km.  Marathoners use distances from 
400m – to several 10s of kilometers.  Also used are training loads lasting more than 2hrs.   
 
In sports walking, running as well as walking are used for short and long distances.  For 
women specializing in the 10km walk, the distances vary from 1-20km, and for 20 and 
50km men walkers—from  1-30km.  The latter as well as marathoners, do training work 
lasting more than 2hrs.   
 
After competition a general picture of the means and methods of developing anaerobic 
and aerobic abilities used in cyclical sports that require endurance is revealed.  In general 
terms, we will present experimental material which shows the range of transfer of the 
physical abilities in the middle, long and super long running distances as well as in sports 
walking for the 10 (women), and 20 and 50km (men) events. 
 
In the men’s and women’s 800m run, there is a range of transfer of physical abilities 
beginning with the 60m run from a low start and ending with the 5000m run (tables 89, 
97).  The latter distances with the men, had a place on two levels of sports mastery 
(1:56:00-2:00:00 and 1:52:00 1:56:00) and with the women, on one level (2:15:00-
2:20:00).  The greatest amounts of correlational interrelationship were fixed in the 400, 
600, and 1000m runs.  In performers of both sexes, the correlation varied from 0.700-
0.900.  In men, the biggest transfer was with the 1000m run (0.912, 0.876, 0.905, 0.856).  
A sharp decrease in the amount of correlational interrelationship was observed in the 
1500m run in men and women.  A weak interrelationship was seen with the 3000 and 
500m runs. 
 
The range of transfer of physical abilities in the men’s 1500m run begins with the 60m 
segment and ends with the 5000m distance.  The cumulative effect has a place on all 
127 "}, {"page": 145, "text": "levels of sports mastery.  In women, as in the men, the range of transfer begins with the 
60m but ends on the 10,000m distance.  In the latter case it appears on three of the five 
levels of sports mastery.  The greatest amount of correlational interrelationship is 
observed in participants of both sexes in the 800, 1000 and 3000m runs (table 90, 98).   
 
Results of the correlational analysis of 800 and 1500m runners shows that with an 
increase in the competitive distance, the range of transfer of physical abilities increases.  
Thus, for men participants in the “long sprint” (800m) transfer is seen with the 5000m 
distance, and in the women specializing in the 1500m run, transfer has a place in the 
10,000m distance.  In the 800m runners greatest transfer was seen with the 600 and 
1000m and with the 1500m runners, in the 800, 1000, and 3000m runs. 
 
In comparing the amounts of interrelationship between results in the competitive running 
distance with women specializing in the 800 and 1500m, we came to the conclusion that 
in the 800m runners, results in the 1500m run were more transferable to the competitive 
event (coefficient of correlation varied from 0.657-0.788), than in the 1500m runners 
(from 0.380-0.652).   
 
Analysis of the results of the ten strongest 800 and 1500m runners in the world 
throughout the history of track and field, shows that the world record holders in the 
1500m run frequently demonstrate a higher level of achievement in the 800m run than 
world record holders in the 800m run in the 1500m distance.  Only one athlete, S. Coe 
was able to have a world record in both distances. 
 
The range of transfer of physical abilities in steeplechase runners begins with the 600m 
run (three levels of sports mastery) and ends with the 10,000m run.  A positive transfer is 
not observed with results in the 100 and 400m runs.  The most transferable were the 
3,000 and 5,000m runs.  Here the coefficient of correlation in four instances was greater 
than 0.700 and in one---0.800 (table 91).  In the 600, 800, 1,000, 1,500 and 10,000m runs, 
the coefficient was very low (from 0.356-0.497), which signifies the weak 
interrelationship between the studied indices.  However, some of the strongest athletes 
128 "}, {"page": 146, "text": "show high sports results not only in the 5,000m distance but in the 1,500, 3,000, and 
10,000m.   Note that the leading runner, H. Rono, set the world record in the 5,000, 
10,000m and steeplechase in his time. 
 
In the women’s 3,000m the range of transfer of physical abilities is somewhat greater 
(table 99), than with the steeplechase runners.  Here it begins with the 400m run and ends 
with the 10,000m run.  The positive interrelationship had a place on all levels of the 
segments tested.  Most transfer was in the 1,000, 1,500, and 5,000m runs.  The 
coefficients of correlation varied from 0.725-0.906.  Transfer to the competitive event 
from the 100 and 200m runs were non-existent.  Practice substantiates that many of the 
strongest 3,000m women runners in the world (Olympic and world champions and record 
holders) showed the greatest results in the mixed distances.  Thus, the former world 
record holder in this distance, T. Kazankina, two time Olympic champion in the 1500m 
and one time winner in the 800m and American M. Decker who was world champion in 
the 1500 and 3000m runs.   
 
The range of transfer of physical abilities in the 5000m run, both in the men as in the 
women, begins with the 600m run (table 92, 100).  In men, transfer appears on all levels 
of sports mastery and in women, only on two (16.00-16.30 and 16.30-17.00min).  The 
cumulative effect is also seen in the marathon results. Here it is observed both in the men 
as in the women only on two levels of sports mastery.  The 800, 1000, 1500, 3000 
10,000m and half marathon, show a positive transfer taking place on all levels of sports 
mastery. The greatest transfer appears in the 3,000 and 10,000m run.  In men, the 
coefficient of correlation in these distances was somewhat higher than in the women.  
 
Results of the correlational analysis substantiates that the range of transfer of physical 
abilities in athletes specializing in the 10,000m run begins with results in the 600m run 
and ends with results in the marathon (table 93, 101).  The first distance has a place on 
two consecutive levels (28.00-28.30 and 28.30-29.00min), and the second, on all levels 
from 28.00-34.00min.  In the women, the range of transfer is somewhat less than in the 
men.  It begins with results in the 1,500m run.  However, runners of both sexes show that 
129 "}, {"page": 147, "text": "the greatest coefficient of correlation was in the 5,000m run as well as in the half 
marathon and marathon.  
 
Results of the last ten world record holders in the 5,000 and 10,000m is evidence of the 
fact that only one athlete was able to set a world record in both distances.  This is despite 
the fact that all runners in the 5000 and 10000m show high sports results and also 
frequently run both of these distances in the Olympic games (V. Kotz, L. Viren, M. Ifter 
and others).  It appears that the ten strongest runners in the world in the 5000m in all of 
track and field history, in most cases do not appear as the strongest top ten runners in the 
10,000m.  Here the discussion is of the ten best results shown by the athletes in the 
5,000m and 10,000m.  Also, the ten strongest runners in the 10,000m rarely enter into the 
top group of the strongest runners in the world in the 5,000m.  And here is still another 
interesting fact. In comparing the transfer (coefficients of correlation) results in the 
10,000m run to results in the 5000m run (tables 93, 101) and results in the 5,000m to 
results in the 10000m (tables 92, 100), it can be seen that in the first case, the coefficients 
of correlation are somewhat higher than in the second. 
 
The range of transfer of physical abilities in men marathoners begins with the 5000m run 
and in the women with the 3000m run (tables 94, 102).  In the men, the cumulative effect 
in the 5000m distance is observed on all levels of sports mastery and in the women, in the 
3000m run only on two beginning levels (2:55:00-3:05:00 and 3:05:00-3:15:00).  Most 
transfer was seen from the 10,000m run and the half marathon.  The coefficient of 
correlation for women as for the men, varied from 0.700-0.800 and more.   
 
Results of the strongest marathoners over the last five Olympic cycles is evidence of the 
fact that not one of the men was able to establish a world record in the 10,000m and be 
victorious in the marathon.  However, some of the strongest 10,000m runners in the 
world (K. Lopesh), by switching to the marathon became Olympic champion.  A 
somewhat different picture is seen with the women.  G. Waitz set a world record in the 
marathon four times, two times in the 3000m, one time each in cross country at the 15km, 
10 and 20mile distances, and likewise, in the half marathon.  Another outstanding 
130 "}, {"page": 148, "text": "woman, I. Christianson was world record holder in the marathon and also in the 5,000 
and 10,000m.  
 
As a rule, most of the strongest world marathon runners show high results in the 10,000m 
run.  This is explained first of all by the fact that almost all of them began by specializing 
in long distance running and only later, after the passage of time, went over to the 
marathon.  In bettering their sports results in the marathon they also improved their 
results in the 10,000m run.  But none of them set a record at this distance during this 
time.  Besides this, in most cases the time (year) of setting personal bests in both 
distances did not coincide. 
 
In athletes specializing in the 10km walk, the cumulative effect was fixed at two running 
distances (5,000 and 10,000m) and in the 1 and 5km walks (table 103).  The cumulative 
effect was absent only on one level of sports results (the 5,000m run).  In the running 
exercises the coefficient of correlation in all cases was very low---from 0.354 up to 0.387 
which shows the weak interrelationship between indices in the 5,000 and 10,000m run 
with the competitive event.  In the 1km walk, it varied on the level of 0.700-0.800.  In the 
5km walk, the coefficient of correlation in three cases exceeded 0.800 and in one, 0.700.   
 
The range of transfer of physical abilities in athletes specializing in the 20km walk begins 
with special developmental exercises and results in the 1km walk and ends with results in 
the 50km walk (table 95).  The cumulative effect also has a place in the 10,000m run.  
The biggest coefficients of correlation were fixed in the 10km walk and the smallest in 
the run at this distance—from  0.354-0.387.  In the 50km walkers, the transfer of physical 
abilities to the 1km walk is observed on two levels of sports mastery and in the 5, 10, and 
20km walks on all levels (table 96).  Most transfer was with the results in the 10 and 
20km walks.  A weak correlation of the interrelationship was observed with indices in the 
10,000m run. 
 
Results of the correlational analysis of athletes specializing in the 20 and 50km walks 
show that in the first group, results in the 10 and 50km have the greatest transfer while 
131 "}, {"page": 149, "text": "for the second group (50km) results in the 10 and 20km walks.  Almost the same was the 
cumulative effect with achievements in the 10,000m run and 1km walk.  Here, the 
coefficient of correlation in all instances did not go above 0.400, which indicates the 
weak interrelationship between them.

ularities or are such results due to the 
system of training used?   
 
We think that the reason for the non-coinciding of the top limits of acquiring maximum 
aerobic and anaerobic productivity acquisition, where the first (aerobic) decreases long 
before the appearance of the second (anaerobic), appear as unknown regularities in the 
development and maintenance of sports form.  This concept was developed in the 
specifics of the so called “hetero-chronicity” (not occurring at the same time) principle of 
sports training in regard to the flow of adaptational processes, restoration of different 
functional abilities of the body systems and so on. We believe that with time, specialists 
will study this question and that in the theory and methods of physical education, the 
truth will be brought out which shows the false presuppositions. 
 
We will close on this looking at the transferable and non-transferable factors when using 
different types of training loads.  We will note that according to the experimental studies, 
we were unable to get experimental data to reveal the essence of the interrelationship 
between the competitive and specialized-developmental exercises with specialized-
preparatory exercises (strength, jump, throws and so on).  This is explained by the fact 
that these latter forms of exercises in sports practice are used sporadically and are far 
from being used by all athletes.  There is also an absence of individual test results in the 
means of speed-strength preparation with the use of strength, jump and throw exercises.  
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - 
157 "}, {"page": 175, "text": " 
The data received by us makes it possible to make several conclusions touching on the 
question of transfer of the cumulative effect from one type of exercise to another.  We 
will begin with the speed-strength exercises.  In all instances there is a positive 
interrelationship between the competitive event and specialized-developmental exercises.  
Positive transfer of physical abilities in the track and field throws had a place on all levels 
of sports mastery when using lighter and heavier implements in the total or complete 
movement. Specialized-preparatory exercises have a positive influence on an increase in 
the sports result in the basic event but up to a specific level of sports mastery.  Further on, 
they do not show a positive effect.   
 
However, in this case it does not mean that specialized-preparatory exercises should be 
excluded from the training.  In our view, it is necessary to use them but to a somewhat 
lesser volume to maintain the achieved level, as well as for carrying out restorative 
measures.  It is very possible that with time, other methods of developing physical 
abilities will be proposed which will widen the range of transfer with the specialized-
preparatory exercises to the competitive and specialized-developmental exercises.  
Specialized-preparatory exercises can appear as “stimulational factors” which on the 
brain level, create conditions for the transfer to the main movement. 
 
In cyclical exercises that require the display of endurance, we have a definite range of 
transfer of physical abilities.  As a rule, in comparison to the competitive event, it begins 
with shorter distances and ends with longer distances.  The exceptions here appear to be 
the ultra long distances (running, walking), where it is impossible to fix the results in 
events that go beyond the competitive distance (marathon, 10km walk -- women, 50km -- 
men).  The presence of a wide range of transfer of physical abilities in each event 
requiring the display of endurance, once again substantiates that in order to achieve a 
definite level of sports results, it is necessary to master one or another form of aerobic 
and anaerobic productivity.  They must correspond to the middle, long and ultra long 
distances in a specific manner.

# Three Competing Theories of Training Transfer: Specifist, Generalist, Holistic

**What it is** — Bondarchuk frames the entire theory of training transfer as a debate
between three schools (PDF pp. 20-28, printed pp. 3-11):
- **Specifists** (traced to E.L. Thorndike's "theory of identical elements," cited as
  ref [223]): transfer between two activities happens only to the degree the activities
  share identical elements (muscle groups, coordination structure, biomechanics). No
  shared elements, no transfer. (PDF p. 20, printed p. 3.)
- **Generalists** (dominant 1940-1960, per the text): argue for the "unity of general and
  specialized preparation" — build a broad general base first (a multi-year "base stage"
  of 4-6 years), then specialize. Bondarchuk reports this view was later revised once
  research showed general-preparation means only build a base for **low-level** athletes;
  for high-level athletes, transfer to the competitive event comes only through
  specialized-preparation means (citing refs [34, 57, 182]). (PDF pp. 22-24, printed pp.
  5-7.)
- **Holistics**: the body acts as one system, so any exercise affects the whole body's
  systems to some degree (non-specific reactions of the heart-circulatory/respiratory
  systems from any cyclical exercise, e.g. rowing or cycling helping a middle-distance
  runner's aerobic base). Bondarchuk explicitly rejects the holistics' full conclusion
  ("it is not possible to agree with the conclusions of the holistics") but keeps their
  narrower point about non-specific systemic reactions, and credits the "block method"
  (physical-preparation block before a technical-preparation block) as the holistics'
  practical answer to sequencing. (PDF pp. 26-28, printed pp. 9-11.)

**Why it works** — The author does not resolve these into a single mechanism in this
section; he uses the three-way split to set up why transfer is contested territory before
he presents his own correlational data in Chapter 2. **Inference:** the specifist view is
the closest ancestor of what this library already holds as
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining, Verkhoshansky/Siff)
and of Verkhoshansky's Principle of Dynamic Correspondence taught in HHPR 5355
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power"); the generalist/holistic debate maps onto
the general-preparation-vs-specialization sequencing question this library already tracks
via Bompa's multilateral development model (vault, not yet cross-checked in this batch).

**When to apply** — Use this three-way split as a diagnostic when reading any other
S&C source's claim about "general" vs "specific" training: ask which of the three
positions it is implicitly taking. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 teaches exercise
selection on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation to
competitive exercises (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`) — that is functionally a generalist-then-
specifist sequencing, not a pure specifist position, and this entry gives Eric's course
material a named theoretical lineage (Thorndike/specifist vs. the generalist sequencing
debate) that the transcript itself does not cite.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported, not proven.** This is Bondarchuk's own
literature synthesis of a decades-old Soviet-era academic debate among track and field
scientists, not an independently replicated finding, and the book gives no citation for
exactly how "generalist" views were falsified beyond two bracketed reference numbers
([34, 57, 182]) this ingest did not chase down. The population behind all three positions
is elite Soviet track and field athletes; extending any of the three views to football
programming (e.g., "GPP only helps low-level players") is Inference, not something this
passage states.

**Example** — A coach who says "just build a big general base before specializing" is
taking the classical generalist position Bondarchuk says was already revised by the
1970s-80s once high-level athlete data showed general work stops producing transfer past
a certain qualification level; see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] for the Chapter 2 data behind that
revision.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining,
staging) — the specifist position's closest modern-book relative in this library.
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the exercise taxonomy this book actually
uses to operationalize the specifist/generalist tension.

# Training Transfer Comes in Four Flavors: Positive, Negative, Neutral, and Indifferent

**What it is** — Bondarchuk names three standard types of training transfer plus a fourth
he flags as rarer and specific to high-level athletes (PDF pp. 31-32, printed pp. 14-15):
- **Positive**: an increase in one exercise's result parallels an increase in another.
- **Negative**: an increase in preparation for one exercise coincides with a decrease in
  another.
- **Neutral** (also "indifferent" in some literature he cites): no measurable effect
  either way.
- **Indifferent/double effect** (his own added category, "met more rarely," specifically
  in high-level athletes using a complex of different exercises): one exercise can help
  and hurt at the same time along different dimensions, e.g. heavier-implement throws
  positive for strength but negative for technique — "there is a noticeable worsening of
  technique in some throws with the use of heavier implements" (refs [18, 152]). Bondarchuk
  gives a specific example: race walkers doing high volumes of aerobic/anaerobic running in
  general preparation showed improved heart-circulatory/respiratory function but worsened
  walking technique (ref [94]), a case of positive-physiological/negative-technical
  double effect. (PDF p. 32, printed p. 15.)

**Why it works** — The positive/negative/neutral categorization itself is a long-standing,
independently established construct in the broader transfer-of-learning literature
(traced by the author himself to E.L. Thorndike's identical-elements theory, cited earlier
in Chapter 1) and is not unique to this book. **This entry keeps the book's `supported`
ceiling** because Bondarchuk's specific fourth category (double/indifferent effect) and
his worked examples are his own, uncross-checked additions, not independently verified
findings. **Inference:** the "double effect" category is a useful naming for something
coaches see constantly (an exercise that builds capacity while degrading movement
quality) but that most popular S&C literature collapses into a vague "watch the technique
cost" warning rather than naming as its own transfer category.

**When to apply** — Use the four-way split as a checklist when introducing a new
exercise: is the expected effect positive, negative, neutral, or a **double effect**
where it will help one quality while hurting another (most often physical capacity up,
technique down, from overloaded implements/loads)? The walking example is the clean
illustration — flag any high-volume general-conditioning block for a technical,
timing-sensitive sport skill (sprinting, throwing, agility) as a double-effect risk, not
just a "general conditioning is fine" default.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The category examples given (heavier
implements degrading throw technique, aerobic-volume race walkers losing walking
technique) are drawn from Soviet-era track and field research cited only by bracketed
reference number [18, 94, 152], not verified against the original sources in this ingest.
Population is elite track and field throwers and race walkers; extending "double effect"
reasoning to football (e.g., heavy sled work degrading sprint mechanics) is Inference,
plausible by analogy but not something this passage tests.

**Example** — **Inference:** a college lineman doing high-volume heavy sled pushes for
GPP strength may show a positive effect on force production and a negative (double)
effect on start technique and shin angle if the sled load or volume is not periodically
reduced back toward the competitive movement pattern, echoing the walker's aerobic-volume
example here.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining,
staging) — the mechanism this claim's negative-transfer cases plausibly run through
(mismatch on one of the ten specificity dimensions).

# Transfer Runs in a Chain: General to Specialized-Preparatory to Specialized-Developmental to Competitive

**What it is** — Bondarchuk describes training transfer as flowing through an ordered
chain of exercise classes rather than any exercise being able to transfer to any other:
"first is the influence of general developmental exercises on specialized-preparatory,
specialized-developmental, or competitive exercises. Second, is the effect of
specialized-preparatory exercises on specialized-developmental and competitive exercises.
Third are training questions on the effect of specialized-developmental exercises on the
competitive event." (PDF p. 33, printed p. 16.) He also notes transfer holds "within the
limits of one exercise" across joint angles or conditions (training leg extensors at one
joint angle transfers to other angles; throwing the full implement transfers to throwing
from a standing position; jumps with a full run-up transfer to short-run-up speed), and
"within the confines of whole motor actions" across related competitive events (an 800m
runner's training affects 400m and 1500m results). (PDF pp. 33-34, printed pp. 16-17.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given beyond the chain's own logic: exercises closer
to the competitive movement (in the classification given in
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]) share more of the competitive event's
"identical elements" (see the specifist position in
[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]), so influence should flow
"downstream" toward more specific exercises more reliably than "upstream." **Inference:**

# "Current" vs. "Distant" Transfer: When in a Training Block the Earlier Work Actually Pays Off

**What it is** — Bondarchuk proposes that when a training cycle is built in successive
stages/blocks, the achieved level from a previous stage can transfer to the following
stage in one of three ways (PDF pp. 35-38, printed pp. 18-21):
1. **Transfer at the start** of the next stage/block — the previous stage's result can
   then be allowed to decrease, increase, or hold, because it already did its job of
   creating the "base."
2. **Transfer in the middle** of the next stage/block — the previous level must be
   actively maintained (not allowed to drop) while the next stage's exercises are
   developed, using reduced-volume maintenance work.
3. **Transfer at the end** of the next stage/block — the previous stage's level must be
   held all the way through.

He then names two broader modes across an entire multi-stage cycle: **"distant" transfer**
(entering sports form in one exercise class first, other classes only later — harder to
manage because you must simultaneously maintain the earlier gains and build the later
ones) versus **"current" (flowing) transfer** (all exercise classes reach sports form
together, because a consistent, unbroken mix of general/specialized-preparatory/
specialized-developmental/competitive exercises runs throughout every stage rather than
being introduced and dropped stage by stage). Current transfer is associated with
variational, combinational, and complex methods of cycle construction; distant transfer
with the stricter stage/block methods. (PDF pp. 41-42, 66-67, printed pp. 24-25, 49-50.)
He also states that excluding specialized-developmental and competitive exercises for more
than 3-4 weeks under the variational method causes a real loss of the previously achieved
level. (PDF p. 38, printed p. 21.)

**Why it works** — No physiological mechanism is offered; this is a purely descriptive,
practice-derived model the author says he arrived at by observing which cycle-construction
methods succeeded ("we came to the conclusion that..."), with no cited independent
verification or controlled comparison in the excerpted text. **Inference:** the "current
transfer" mode maps loosely onto what Western periodization literature calls concurrent or
conjugate training (train all qualities across the whole cycle, in varying proportions)
versus "distant transfer" mapping onto strict block/linear periodization (sequential
single-quality phases) — a connection this passage does not make itself.

**When to apply** — Use as a lens for diagnosing a specific periodization complaint: if
an athlete's speed or strength level noticeably drops during a technical or in-season
phase, ask whether the program is using a "distant transfer" model (which requires
active, planned maintenance work for the earlier-built quality) without actually
including that maintenance work. **Eric's baseline:** in-season programming at Baylor
follows "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than continuing to build strength
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`) — that is functionally the "transfer in
the middle" case above (actively holding a previously-built level while a new emphasis
develops), though the course material does not use Bondarchuk's terminology.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This is presented in the text as the
author's own unverified conclusion from practical observation, not tested against a
control condition or independently replicated, and the book gives no citation trail for
it at all (unusual for this chapter, which otherwise cites bracketed references
throughout). Treat this as a plausible practitioner heuristic, not an established finding.
Population is elite Soviet track and field athletes on multi-decade national training
cycles; applying the three-situations timing model to a much shorter college football
in-season/off-season calendar is Inference.

**Example** — A discus thrower doing a strength-emphasis GPP block followed by a
technical/competition block: under "current transfer," strength work continues at reduced
volume throughout the technical block so the strength level is still rising (or at least
held) when the athlete peaks technically; under "distant transfer" with poor execution,
strength work is dropped entirely once the technical block starts and the athlete arrives
at competition weaker than at the end of GPP.

**Related** — [[heuristic--general-prep-stage-duration-must-match-sports-form-cycle]] —
the companion finding on how stage duration interacts with whether transfer can happen at
all.

# A General-Preparation Stage Only "Counts" If It Lasts as Long as the Athlete's Own Sports-Form Cycle

**What it is** — Bondarchuk states that most athletes, after a rest/transition period,
take 2-3 months to enter a state of "sports form" in whatever exercises they are doing,
though some individuals take 4-8 months. A general-preparation stage/block can only
function as a real "base" or "foundation" for the following specialized stage if it lasts
at least as long as that individual's own sports-form development timeline. He gives a
worked counter-example: a sprint/hurdle program with a 10-day general-endurance stage, a
15-day general-strength stage, a 6-8 week speed/speed-endurance stage, and a 2-3 week
entry-into-form stage. Because the first two stages are far shorter than the 2-3+ months
needed to reach sports form, he argues it is "impossible to resolve" real development of
general endurance or general strength in that time — those stages become mere "followers"
(tag-alongs) that prep the body for the next stage, not genuine developmental blocks in
their own right, and sports form only actually begins developing once the speed/speed-
endurance stage starts. (PDF pp. 39-40, printed pp. 22-23.) Only stage, block,
stage-variant, and block-variant methods (which run long enough) can create a real
transferable base; very short 1-3 week rotating stages cannot produce "distant" transfer
of a created base — only "current" transfer is possible under those short-cycle designs
(see [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]]). (PDF pp. 40-42, printed pp.
23-25.)

**Why it works** — The claim rests on Bondarchuk's premise (stated, not derived here) that
entering "sports form" for a given exercise complex takes a fairly fixed, athlete-specific
duration (2-3 months typical, up to 8 months for some individuals); a stage shorter than
that duration cannot complete the adaptation cycle it is nominally targeting, so whatever
training happens in it is incidental preparation for the next stage rather than a genuine
developmental phase in itself.

**When to apply** — Use as a sanity check on any periodization plan with short (1-3 week)
"phases" labeled by quality (a "strength phase," a "conditioning phase"): ask whether that
phase is actually long enough, for this athlete population, to produce a real adaptation
in that quality, or whether it is functioning only as a short lead-in to the phase after
it. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 teaches training residual effects that set a
retraining cadence — aerobic capacity and max strength need re-exposure roughly every 30
days, speed roughly every 5 days (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27`) — that is a maintenance-cadence claim,
distinct from but complementary to Bondarchuk's claim here about how long an *initial*
developmental stage must run to create a base in the first place.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The 2-3 month (up to 4-8 month)
sports-form timeline is stated by the author as known "from the literature," without a
specific citation in the excerpted pages, and is drawn from elite Soviet track and field
athletes on year-round training cycles. A college football off-season/summer/fall-camp
calendar is structured very differently (fixed NCAA calendar windows, not free-running
sports-form cycles), so directly importing "your GPP phase must be 2-3 months to count" as
a hard rule for football is Inference — the underlying logic (a phase shorter than the
adaptation timeline for the targeted quality risks being incidental, not developmental)
is more portable than the specific duration numbers.

**Example** — A 2-week "GPP block" before fall camp, by this logic, is very unlikely to
produce genuine general strength or conditioning adaptations in the Bondarchuk sense; it
functions instead as preparation for the next block's actual training stress, and should
be programmed and evaluated as such rather than credited with building a real strength or
conditioning "base."

**Related** — [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]] — the transfer-timing
model this duration rule directly feeds. [[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]]
(Supertraining, staging) — the general-preparation/work-capacity concept this stage
duration question applies to.

# Bondarchuk Publishes 34 Normative Tables Linking Assistance-Exercise Results to Competitive-Result Bands, by Age and Qualification

**What it is** — Tables 1-34 (PDF pp. 44-67, printed pp. 27-50; this ingest sampled
representative tables rather than transcribing all 34) give normative "model
characteristics": for a given competitive-result band (e.g., 100m in 10.00-10.20s vs.
10.80-11.00s), a matching range of expected results in assistance exercises. Examples
pulled directly: **Table 1** ties 100m sprint splits (10m through 100m segments) to
five 100m-time bands. **Table 2** ties speed-strength markers (standing long jump,
triple/5-fold/10-fold jump from place, single-leg and alternate-leg jumps for time) to
those same five 100m bands — e.g., a 10.00-10.20s sprinter should stand-long-jump
3.10-3.30m, a 10.80-11.00s sprinter 2.70-2.90m. Similar tables exist for 200m, 400m,
women's 100m hurdles, and age-banded (15-16 / 17-18 / 19+) versions for 400m men and
women across successive preparatory/competitive periods (Tables 10-14). Table 8 also
gives named-athlete individual data (L. Evans, T. Smith, V. Markin, and others) tying
100m/200m/repeated-200m splits to final 400m results and a derived "speed reserve"
metric (400m result minus the doubled 200m split, e.g. L. Evans: 0.765s reserve).
(PDF pp. 44-51, printed pp. 27-34.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given; these are purely descriptive normative
benchmarks compiled from the author's dataset, presented as targets an athlete "should"
hit at a given competitive level, not as evidence of a causal relationship. **Inference:**
this functions the same way modern S&C "standards tables" (e.g., a vertical-jump-by-40-
time chart) function — useful as a rough talent-identification or gap-analysis tool, not
as proof that improving the assistance-exercise number will improve the competitive time.

**When to apply** — Use as a historical reference point or sanity check when building
Baylor's own sport-specific normative tables (a named gap in `method-baseline.md`,
"Testing and assessment," citing `performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase
2`): Bondarchuk's tables show what a rigorous, qualification-banded normative table looks
like (multiple assistance exercises per competitive-result band, banded by age where
relevant), even though the specific numbers are 1970s-80s Soviet track and field data and
not directly usable for a 2026 football roster.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, and only as a description that these
tables exist and roughly what they show — this entry does not treat any individual number
as validated for use as a current standard. The population is elite/sub-elite Soviet-era
male and female track and field athletes (refs [52], [74], [75] per the tables), not
football players; the specific split times, jump distances, and the Table 8 "speed
reserve" formula are Inference if applied to any other sport or era without
re-derivation. This ingest did not transcribe all 34 tables (only Tables 1-14 were pulled
in full); a future batch revisiting this chapter should note that gap before citing a
table number 15-34 that was not directly checked here.

**Example** — A recruiting or testing-standards project comparing "where does our sprinter
sit" could borrow the *format* (competitive-result band -> matching assistance-exercise
range, split by age where useful) from Table 2/10-14 without adopting the actual Soviet-
era numbers.

# Two Test Families: "General" Tests Shared Across Events, "Specialized" Tests Unique to Each

**What it is** — Bondarchuk splits the tests used to study training transfer into two
families (PDF pp. 68-69, printed pp. 51-52):
- **General tests**: not tests of general-preparatory exercises specifically, but tests
  "used in mixed groups or between groups" — i.e., shared across many events. For
  heart-circulatory/respiratory function, nearly identical tests are used across all of
  track and field (max oxygen uptake on a veloergometer, time-to-exhaustion at max VO2,
  anaerobic threshold). For speed-strength sports, common general tests are the 60m run
  from blocks, barbell snatch, half squat with barbell, standing long jump, vertical jump
  (Abalakov method), triple jump from place, and forward/backward shot throws.
- **Specialized tests**: tests unique to each event's specific demands, most reliably
  results in **specialized-developmental exercises** — i.e., the competitive movement
  itself executed under lighter or more difficult conditions (lighter/heavier implements
  in throws, shorter approach runs in jumps, varied segment/rest combinations in cyclical
  events). He states specialized-developmental test reliability is the best-established
  of the test types; general-preparatory and specialized-preparatory test reliability is
  explicitly flagged as "not fully confirmed" and something to be "tightened up in the
  near future." (PDF p. 69, printed p. 52.)

**Why it works** — The logic follows directly from
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]]: since specialized-developmental
exercises sit closest to the competitive event in the transfer chain, tests built from
those same exercises should track competitive readiness more reliably than tests built
from more general exercises further from the competitive movement.

**When to apply** — When designing or auditing a testing battery, prioritize tests that
are themselves specialized-developmental-class movements (the competitive skill under
altered load/distance conditions) over generic strength/power tests when the goal is
tracking competitive readiness specifically; reserve the generic tests (snatch, squat,
vertical jump, etc.) for tracking general physical qualities, which the author himself
says have less-confirmed reliability as *transfer* indicators even though they are
common practice.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own
methodological framing for the correlational study that follows in Chapter 2, presented
without a formal reliability study of his own two test families in the excerpted pages
(he cites "already been shown" reliability for specialized-developmental tests, but gives
no reference number here). Population is Soviet track and field testing practice of the
1970s-80s; the specific listed general tests (barbell snatch, Abalakov jump, etc.) reflect
that era's tools, not necessarily current force-plate/GPS-based options. Applying the
general/specialized test distinction to Baylor's own battery design (`method-baseline.md`,
"Testing and assessment") is Inference in terms of which specific tests to pick, though
the underlying logic (prefer tests closest to the competitive movement for readiness
tracking) is directly portable.

**Example** — For a football wide receiver, a "specialized" test in this framework would
be a competitive-adjacent movement under altered conditions (e.g., a route run against a
lighter or heavier resistance band, or a shortened-approach vertical jump), while a
"general" test would be a standard vertical jump or broad jump shared across every
position group.

**Related** — [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — the transfer logic
this test-selection framework is built on.

# Two Test Families: "General" Tests Shared Across Events, "Specialized" Tests Unique to Each

**What it is** — Bondarchuk splits the tests used to study training transfer into two
families (PDF pp. 68-69, printed pp. 51-52):
- **General tests**: not tests of general-preparatory exercises specifically, but tests
  "used in mixed groups or between groups" — i.e., shared across many events. For
  heart-circulatory/respiratory function, nearly identical tests are used across all of
  track and field (max oxygen uptake on a veloergometer, time-to-exhaustion at max VO2,
  anaerobic threshold). For speed-strength sports, common general tests are the 60m run
  from blocks, barbell snatch, half squat with barbell, standing long jump, vertical jump
  (Abalakov method), triple jump from place, and forward/backward shot throws.
- **Specialized tests**: tests unique to each event's specific demands, most reliably
  results in **specialized-developmental exercises** — i.e., the competitive movement
  itself executed under lighter or more difficult conditions (lighter/heavier implements
  in throws, shorter approach runs in jumps, varied segment/rest combinations in cyclical
  events). He states specialized-developmental test reliability is the best-established
  of the test types; general-preparatory and specialized-preparatory test reliability is
  explicitly flagged as "not fully confirmed" and something to be "tightened up in the
  near future." (PDF p. 69, printed p. 52.)

**Why it works** — The logic follows directly from
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]]: since specialized-developmental
exercises sit closest to the competitive event in the transfer chain, tests built from
those same exercises should track competitive readiness more reliably than tests built
from more general exercises further from the competitive movement.

**When to apply** — When designing or auditing a testing battery, prioritize tests that
are themselves specialized-developmental-class movements (the competitive skill under
altered load/distance conditions) over generic strength/power tests when the goal is
tracking competitive readiness specifically; reserve the generic tests (snatch, squat,
vertical jump, etc.) for tracking general physical qualities, which the author himself
says have less-confirmed reliability as *transfer* indicators even though they are
common practice.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own
methodological framing for the correlational study that follows in Chapter 2, presented
without a formal reliability study of his own two test families in the excerpted pages
(he cites "already been shown" reliability for specialized-developmental tests, but gives
no reference number here). Population is Soviet track and field testing practice of the
1970s-80s; the specific listed general tests (barbell snatch, Abalakov jump, etc.) reflect
that era's tools, not necessarily current force-plate/GPS-based options. Applying the
general/specialized test distinction to Baylor's own battery design (`method-baseline.md`,
"Testing and assessment") is Inference in terms of which specific tests to pick, though
the underlying logic (prefer tests closest to the competitive movement for readiness
tracking) is directly portable.

**Example** — For a football wide receiver, a "specialized" test in this framework would
be a competitive-adjacent movement under altered conditions (e.g., a route run against a
lighter or heavier resistance band, or a shortened-approach vertical jump), while a
"general" test would be a standard vertical jump or broad jump shared across every
position group.

**Related** — [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — the transfer logic
this test-selection framework is built on.

# Correlation Can Hide a "Tie-In" Exercise That Is Actually Doing the Work

**What it is** — Bondarchuk describes his standard method for the whole book: statistical
analysis (correlation, regression, dispersion, factor analysis, multiple correlation) of
interrelationships between results in different training exercises, using a minimum of
5-6 indices per athlete group because a single pairwise correlation "does not always
reflect the true essence of the interaction." (PDF p. 70, printed p. 53.) He then gives a
single illustrative case (his own words: "we will illustrate with one example"): a training
session using three exercises, A, B, and C in sequence. After an experiment, results
improved in A and C but not in B. A high correlation between A and B suggested (wrongly)
that B was ineffective or non-transferring. A follow-up experiment dropped B and trained
only A and C — and this time **neither A nor C improved**. Bondarchuk's interpretation:
exercise B had a "tie-in effect," stimulating the positive transfer between A and C even
though B itself showed no measurable within-exercise result and its own pairwise
correlation to A/C looked unremarkable. (PDF pp. 70-71, printed pp. 53-54.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is proposed beyond the observation itself; Bondarchuk
explicitly defers this to "additional studies" that "will resolve this interaction." The
described method (pairwise correlation across a sequence of exercises) is structurally
blind to exactly this kind of three-way interaction, since it only measures direct
pairwise relationships, not an exercise's indirect enabling effect on the relationship
between two *other* exercises.

**When to apply** — Use as a standing caution whenever a program change removes an
exercise because it looks "ineffective" by direct correlation or by the athlete's own
result in that exercise not improving: check whether removing it changes the trajectory
of other exercises in the same session/block before concluding it added nothing. This is
a genuinely underused idea in practical programming, where "cut what isn't working" is a
common simplification heuristic that this example directly complicates.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This entire finding rests on a single
worked example ("we will address only one of the situations") with no stated sample size,
no statistical test, and no independent replication in the excerpted text — it is
presented by the author himself as an open question for future research, not a settled
result. Do not cite this as evidence that any specific exercise combination has a tie-in
effect; treat it only as a methodological caution about what pairwise correlation studies
(including Bondarchuk's own Chapter 2 tables) cannot detect. Population and exercises A/B/C
are unspecified in the text (not named events or lifts), so there is nothing concrete to
generalize from besides the logical structure of the example.

**Example** — **Inference:** a strength coach who drops an unweighted plyometric drill
from a sprint-training session because the drill's own jump-height numbers aren't
improving might, per this heuristic, want to check whether removing it also flattens the
sprint-speed gains the program was otherwise seeing — the drill could be a tie-in exercise
even though its own metric looks stagnant.

**Related** — No existing library entry addresses this specific correlation blind spot;
flag for cross-reference if a future ingest (e.g., a sports-statistics or research-methods
source) covers interaction effects or mediation more formally.

# Bondarchuk's Own Four Exercise Classes, in His Own Words: General Preparatory, Specialized-Preparatory, Specialized-Developmental, Competitive

**What it is** — This is the primary-source definition of the classification this book's
own title concept depends on, drawn from Bondarchuk's Glossary (not from Chapter 2's
prose, which assumes the reader already knows these terms):
- **General (Preparatory) Exercises / GPP**: "do not repeat the competitive actions as a
  whole or their separate parts. Other muscle groups take part in the work being done. The
  functional systems of the body are activated but do not ensure an increase in results in
  the competitive exercise." Function: all-round development, work capacity, and active
  rest/restoration. (PDF p. 12, printed p. x.)
- **Specialized-Preparatory Exercises / SPP**: like general exercises, "do not repeat the
  competitive actions as a whole or in their separate parts. However, they use similar
  muscle groups in their execution," activating the functions and body systems the main
  movement depends on, with "identical or close to identical regimes of muscle work."
  (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Specialized-Developmental Exercises / SDE**: "repeat the competitive exercise in its
  separate parts. In executing them, one and the same muscle groups participate, together
  with activation of similar systems and organs. They not only repeat the muscle work
  regime and other systems of the body... but also supersede them," and "serve for entry
  into the state of sports form." (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Competitive Exercises / CE**: "the acting definition... is 'sport event,' in which the
  athlete participates in competition," executed either in actual competition or in
  training as a model/repeat of competitive conditions, easier or harder. (PDF p. 12,
  printed p. x-xi.)
Chapter 2's own intro adds a cross-cutting distinction independent of the four classes: a
**local** exercise (uses separate parts/body links — squat, bench press, standing long
jump, vertical jump) versus a **global** exercise (uses all body links together — the
barbell clean). (PDF p. 75, printed p. 58.)

**Why it works** — The four classes form an ordered continuum of how much of the
competitive movement (muscle groups, movement structure, muscle-work regime) an exercise
reproduces, which is the same logic underlying
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and the specifist "identical
elements" position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]: more shared
elements with the competitive movement should predict more reliable positive transfer.
Chapter 2's correlational data (see the claim entries below) is this book's attempt to
test that prediction empirically, event by event.

**When to apply** — Use as the primary-source definition when auditing any exercise
selection against this taxonomy, in place of or alongside secondary paraphrases of it.
**Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in HHPR 5355 is taught "on a spectrum from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of 'sport specific'"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`; `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`) — this entry
gives that course material its primary-source citation and exact definitions. This
library already has a secondary-source treatment of the same taxonomy in
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault), built from Moyer's course paraphrase rather than Bondarchuk's own text; that
entry's table ("GPE/SPE/SDE/CE") matches this one closely but labels Moyer's own sprint
examples (bounding, banded pawback, etc.), not Bondarchuk's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, not proven: this is Bondarchuk's own
classification scheme, widely adopted in the Soviet/Russian sport-science tradition and
cross-referenced by Verkhoshansky's circle (see the Related links), but it is a
practitioner taxonomy, not an independently tested causal model, and the boundary between
classes is fuzzy in application (the Moyer-derived entry below makes the same point about
sprint exercises specifically). The four-class definitions here are written for individual
track and field events; a football skill (e.g., a pass rush) is a much less discrete,
single "competitive exercise" than a 100m sprint or a hammer throw, so classifying a given
drill as SPP vs. SDE for football is Inference, not something Bondarchuk's glossary
addresses.

**Example** — For a shot putter: general preparatory = general conditioning running;
specialized-preparatory = barbell snatch, half squat (same leg-extensor muscle groups,
different movement); specialized-developmental = throwing a lighter or heavier shot
(repeats the throw's parts under altered load); competitive = throwing the 7.26kg
competition shot in a meet.

**Related** — `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault) — the secondary, Moyer-course paraphrase of this same taxonomy; **reciprocal-link
suggestion**: add a note there pointing back to this primary-source entry once this book
clears the review gate. [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — the transfer
logic built on this classification. [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] —
the specifist theory this classification operationalizes.
