# Bondarchuk's Own Four Exercise Classes, in His Own Words: General Preparatory, Specialized-Preparatory, Specialized-Developmental, Competitive

**What it is** — This is the primary-source definition of the classification this book's
own title concept depends on, drawn from Bondarchuk's Glossary (not from Chapter 2's
prose, which assumes the reader already knows these terms):
- **General (Preparatory) Exercises / GPP**: "do not repeat the competitive actions as a
  whole or their separate parts. Other muscle groups take part in the work being done. The
  functional systems of the body are activated but do not ensure an increase in results in
  the competitive exercise." Function: all-round development, work capacity, and active
  rest/restoration. (PDF p. 12, printed p. x.)
- **Specialized-Preparatory Exercises / SPP**: like general exercises, "do not repeat the
  competitive actions as a whole or in their separate parts. However, they use similar
  muscle groups in their execution," activating the functions and body systems the main
  movement depends on, with "identical or close to identical regimes of muscle work."
  (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Specialized-Developmental Exercises / SDE**: "repeat the competitive exercise in its
  separate parts. In executing them, one and the same muscle groups participate, together
  with activation of similar systems and organs. They not only repeat the muscle work
  regime and other systems of the body... but also supersede them," and "serve for entry
  into the state of sports form." (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Competitive Exercises / CE**: "the acting definition... is 'sport event,' in which the
  athlete participates in competition," executed either in actual competition or in
  training as a model/repeat of competitive conditions, easier or harder. (PDF p. 12,
  printed p. x-xi.)
Chapter 2's own intro adds a cross-cutting distinction independent of the four classes: a
**local** exercise (uses separate parts/body links — squat, bench press, standing long
jump, vertical jump) versus a **global** exercise (uses all body links together — the
barbell clean). (PDF p. 75, printed p. 58.)

**Why it works** — The four classes form an ordered continuum of how much of the
competitive movement (muscle groups, movement structure, muscle-work regime) an exercise
reproduces, which is the same logic underlying
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and the specifist "identical
elements" position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]: more shared
elements with the competitive movement should predict more reliable positive transfer.
Chapter 2's correlational data (see the claim entries below) is this book's attempt to
test that prediction empirically, event by event.

**When to apply** — Use as the primary-source definition when auditing any exercise
selection against this taxonomy, in place of or alongside secondary paraphrases of it.
**Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in HHPR 5355 is taught "on a spectrum from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of 'sport specific'"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`; `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`) — this entry
gives that course material its primary-source citation and exact definitions. This
library already has a secondary-source treatment of the same taxonomy in
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault), built from Moyer's course paraphrase rather than Bondarchuk's own text; that
entry's table ("GPE/SPE/SDE/CE") matches this one closely but labels Moyer's own sprint
examples (bounding, banded pawback, etc.), not Bondarchuk's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, not proven: this is Bondarchuk's own
classification scheme, widely adopted in the Soviet/Russian sport-science tradition and
cross-referenced by Verkhoshansky's circle (see the Related links), but it is a
practitioner taxonomy, not an independently tested causal model, and the boundary between
classes is fuzzy in application (the Moyer-derived entry below makes the same point about
sprint exercises specifically). The four-class definitions here are written for individual
track and field events; a football skill (e.g., a pass rush) is a much less discrete,
single "competitive exercise" than a 100m sprint or a hammer throw, so classifying a given
drill as SPP vs. SDE for football is Inference, not something Bondarchuk's glossary
addresses.

**Example** — For a shot putter: general preparatory = general conditioning running;
specialized-preparatory = barbell snatch, half squat (same leg-extensor muscle groups,
different movement); specialized-developmental = throwing a lighter or heavier shot
(repeats the throw's parts under altered load); competitive = throwing the 7.26kg
competition shot in a meet.

logic built on this classification. [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] —
the specifist theory this classification operationalizes.

# Specialized-Developmental Runs (Flying 30m, Blocks 30-200m) Correlate Strongly with Sprint/Hurdle Competitive Results

**What it is** — Tables 41-50 (PDF pp. 78-87, printed pp. 61-70) report correlation
coefficients between competitive results and other specialized-developmental/competitive
run distances, for men's and women's 100m, 200m, 400m, 110m/400m hurdles (men) and
100m/400m hurdles (women), each split by "high level" vs. "low level" athlete
qualification (the table note: high-level in the numerator, low-level in the denominator
for these specific tables — Tables 41-50 only; see the reversed convention noted in
`_book.md` for the throws tables). Bondarchuk's own summary: "the coefficients of
correlation in most cases are in the range of 0.700-0.800" (PDF p. 87, printed p. 70).
Representative individual values pulled directly: 100m runners' 30m-flying-start-to-100m
correlation 0.678/0.778 (high/low, Table 41); 110m hurdlers' 110m-hurdles-to-60m-from-
blocks correlation as low as 0.420 at one qualification level (Table 44); 400m hurdlers'
400m-hurdles-to-600m correlation as high as 0.890 (Table 45).

**Why it works** — No mechanism beyond the transfer-chain logic in
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]]: these are all specialized-
developmental or competitive-class exercises per
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] (shorter/longer runs at or near race
intensity), sharing most of the sprint or hurdle event's biomechanics and energy-system
demands, so high shared-element overlap predicts the observed high correlation.

**When to apply** — Use as historical evidence that assistance runs at varied distances
(flying starts, sub-maximal and supra-maximal segment lengths) are a reliably transferable
training tool for sprint/hurdle athletes, supporting programs that use varied-distance
sprint work rather than only full-distance reps. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355's
linear-sprint testing already uses split-time interpretation by physical quality (0-10m
acceleration, 30-40m speed) rather than total time alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Speed
and sprint," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`) — this book's high
segment-to-total correlations support treating those splits as meaningfully diagnostic,
not just a total-time proxy.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite and sub-elite
Soviet-era male and female sprinters and hurdlers (refs implicit in the tables' athlete
qualification split; exact sample sizes are not given in the excerpted pages). The
correlations described are all between running-based specialized-developmental/
competitive exercises — this entry does NOT cover strength or jump-exercise transfer,
which is markedly weaker (see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]]). Applying these specific
coefficients to football skill-position speed training is Inference: football speed
development sits inside a team-sport context with far less training-time devoted purely
to sprinting than a specialized Soviet track program, so the magnitude of these
correlations should not be assumed to hold as-is.

**Example** — A 200m runner's training program built heavily around 150m and 300m
repeats at race-adjacent intensity is well-supported by this data (150m-to-200m and
300m-to-200m correlations were among the higher entries in Table 42), more so than a
program relying mainly on much shorter (30m) segments for that specific event.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification these
correlated exercises fall into. [[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] —
the much weaker transfer picture for non-running assistance exercises in the same event
group.

# The Barbell Snatch and Half Squat Transfer to Sprinting Only Up to a Narrow, Specific Performance Band, Then Stop

**What it is** — Tables 51-60 (PDF pp. 91-99, printed pp. 74-82) correlate the barbell
snatch and half squat (with barbell on shoulders) against 100m/200m/400m and hurdle
results across five to six performance bands per event. Bondarchuk's own reading: overall
interrelationship is poor, and where a positive ("cumulative") effect exists at all, it is
confined to specific, narrow bands rather than holding across all qualification levels.
Examples with locators: men's 100m snatch/squat "cumulative effect" only up to
11.10-11.40s (Table 51: snatch coefficients range from -0.186 at 10.20-10.50s up to only
0.396 at 11.10-11.40s); women's snatch shows an effect on only one band, 12.70-12.79s
(Table 56); in the 400m hurdles, "a positive interrelationship... was not seen" at all,
with correlation coefficients ranging only 0.196-0.320 (Table 55, printed p. 77, citing
his own summary sentence at PDF p. 89/printed p. 72). Throws of the shot forward/backward
were even weaker transfer exercises, positive only for 110m hurdlers at two narrow bands
(13.50-14.00s and 14.00-14.50s) and absent elsewhere. (PDF pp. 88-90, printed pp. 71-73.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: "the cumulative effect from strength
exercises will appear only when they are close to the competitive event according to the
biomechanical aspects and methodological parameters" (PDF p. 102, printed p. 85) — i.e.
the snatch and squat are specialized-preparatory (per
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]), sharing muscle groups with sprinting but
not its movement structure, velocity, or ground-contact regime, so per
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] they sit further from the competitive
event in the transfer chain than the running-based exercises in
[[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]]. He explicitly declines to
call this "ineffectiveness," instead suggesting the missing transfer could be a
methodological artifact (rep count, session compactness, intensity zones used) rather than
a fixed property of the exercises. (PDF p. 102, printed p. 85.)

**When to apply** — Use as historical caution against assuming barbell strength numbers
(snatch, squat) will keep predicting sprint improvement once an athlete passes a certain
performance level; per this data, once an athlete is already fast, further improvement in
these lifts stops tracking with further sprint improvement. This does not mean drop the
lifts (see [[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for
Bondarchuk's own prescription on that point) — it means stop expecting them to be the
driver of further sprint gains at that point.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite and sub-elite
Soviet-era sprinters/hurdlers, both sexes, tested with a specific barbell snatch and a
half-squat-with-barbell-on-shoulders (not a full back squat, front squat, or trap-bar
variant); the finding should not be assumed to hold for a different strength exercise
variation without its own data. This is track and field data; extending "barbell strength
work plateaus in its transfer to top-end speed past a certain level" to football speed
training is Inference, though it is broadly consistent with general S&C literature on
strength/speed transfer diminishing at higher training ages — that broader literature was
not cross-checked in this ingest.

**Example** — A high-level 100m sprinter already running 10.2-10.4s should not expect
squat or snatch PRs to reliably predict further 100m improvement, per this data; a
developing sprinter in the 11.0-11.5s range is more likely to still be inside the band
where this book's data shows a measurable (if still modest) positive relationship.

**Related** — [[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]] — the much
stronger transfer picture for running-based assistance work in the same event group.
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] — Bondarchuk's own
prescription for what to do once an exercise stops producing further transfer.

with correlation coefficients ranging only 0.196-0.320 (Table 55, printed p. 77, citing

# Among Assistance Exercises, Multi-Jump Work (Ten-Fold Jump, Leg-to-Leg Bounds) Transfers to Sprinting Most Consistently — More Than Single Jumps, Throws, or Barbell Lifts

**What it is** — Comparing all the specialized-preparatory assistance exercises tested
against sprint/hurdle competitive results (barbell snatch, half squat, standing long jump,
vertical jump, triple jump from place, 10-fold jump from place, leg-to-leg jumps for 50m,
forward/backward shot throws), Bondarchuk identifies the **10-fold jump from place** and
**leg-to-leg (bounding) jumps for 50m** as "more transferable than other specialized-
preparatory exercises," measured not by having the single highest correlation coefficient
but by the number of qualification-level bands across which a positive cumulative effect
appears (PDF p. 99, printed p. 82). Concretely: leg-to-leg jumps for 50m showed a
cumulative effect on **all levels** for both men's and women's 100m, and across the full
range for women's 100m hurdles (12.80-15.80s) and men's 400m hurdles (49.50-55.50s) (PDF
p. 100, printed p. 83). By contrast, the standing long jump, vertical jump, and triple
jump from place each showed positive transfer only on two-to-three of five levels for most
events, and high jump/pole vault-style single jumps were even more level-restricted for
sprint events specifically (not their own competitive event). He generalizes: "with an
increase in a number of take-offs when executing the above mentioned jump exercises, there
is an increase in the number of cases of positive transfer" — proposing multi-jump
exercises over long ground-contact segments (20-150m) as the most broadly transferable
jump category for track and field generally. (PDF pp. 100-101, printed pp. 83-84.)

**Why it works** — His own stated mechanism: multi-jump exercises over distance "repeat
the biomechanical parameters of the competitive movement" more closely than single jumps,
"have a similar appearance to the muscle work regimes, and use the same intensity zones,"
and can duplicate the sprint's actual duration/segment structure (e.g. matching a starting-
acceleration segment specifically). (PDF p. 101, printed p. 84.) In the terms of
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], repeated bounding over a real sprint-
relevant distance sits closer to specialized-developmental than a single standing jump
does, which under [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] predicts exactly
the stronger, more level-consistent transfer observed here.

**When to apply** — When choosing between plyometric/jump exercise variants for a
sprint-focused program, this data favors prioritizing repeated multi-jump/bounding work
over set distances (matched to the target phase of the sprint — acceleration vs. max
velocity) over single-effort jumps (standing long jump, vertical jump) as the more
consistently transferable choice, while still using single jumps for their own
diagnostic/training value.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
sprinters and hurdlers, both sexes; "leg-to-leg jumps for 50m" and "10-fold jump from
place" are specific, defined tests in this text, not a stand-in for every modern bounding
or plyometric variation. The claim is about *transfer consistency across qualification
levels*, not about which exercise has the single highest correlation value — do not
conflate the two when citing this entry. Applying this preference (multi-jump over
single-jump assistance work) to football speed/power training is Inference, plausible by
analogy to established plyometric literature but not tested here on a football
population.

**Example** — A sprint-development block choosing between a session of standing long
jumps and a session of 10-15 continuous alternate-leg bounds over 30-50m would, per this
data, expect the bounding session to transfer more reliably across a wider range of athlete
ability levels.

**Related** — [[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]] — the
running-based exercises that transfer even more strongly than jumps in this event group.
[[claim--jump-event-exercise-transfer-patterns]] — the parallel (and partly consistent)
finding for jump-event athletes' own competitive results.

# Jump-from-a-Short-Run-Up Is the Single Most Transferable Assistance Exercise for Every Jump Event; High Jump Is the Outlier

**What it is** — Tables 61-68 (PDF pp. 104-112, printed pp. 87-95) correlate running,
jumping, and strength/throw exercises against long jump, high jump, triple jump, and pole
vault results, men and women. Across long jump, triple jump, and pole vault, **all**
running and jumping exercises showed a cumulative positive effect; the two throwing
exercises (shot forward/backward) showed essentially none. The single strongest, most
consistent exercise across event types was the **jump/vault with a short run-up**: long
jumpers' correlation to a short-approach jump ran as high as 0.890-0.967 (Tables 61-62);
triple jumpers' short-run-up triple jump ran 0.890-0.954 for men, 0.700-0.906 for women
(Table 65-66); pole vaulters' short-run-up vault ran 0.745-0.865 (Tables 67-68). **High
jump was the outlier**: the author states plainly that in men's and women's high jump,
"in all cases, a weak interrelationship between the test results was observed on the
0.400 level" for running exercises specifically — the informative exercise there was
instead the vertical jump with a short run-up (0.876-0.965) and, unusually for a jump
event, the 10-fold jump from place (0.876-0.965, Tables 63-64) rather than the sprint
times that predicted every other jump event well. Barbell snatch showed almost no
transfer anywhere in this section except isolated single-level effects; the half squat
with barbell transferred more consistently, especially for high jump and pole vault (all
levels for both sexes in those two events). (PDF pp. 104-113, printed pp. 87-96.)

**Why it works** — Per [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] and
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]], the short-run-up version of each
event's own competitive movement is itself a specialized-developmental exercise (repeats
the competitive action's parts under an altered, easier condition), so it sits closest to
the competitive event in the transfer chain — consistent with it outperforming
general-preparatory sprint and strength exercises across every jump event tested. High
jump's break from the sprint-correlated pattern of the other three jump events is not
explained mechanistically by the author; **Inference:** the high jump's approach and
takeoff (curved run, back-to-the-bar rotation) differs enough biomechanically from a
straight-line sprint that raw straight-ahead sprint speed may simply share fewer
"identical elements" with it than with long jump, triple jump, or pole vault approaches.

**When to apply** — When selecting assistance work for a jump-event athlete, this data
supports prioritizing a short-approach version of the competitive jump itself as the
highest-value transfer exercise, over generic sprint times or barbell strength numbers,
with the explicit exception of high jump, where multi-jump (10-fold) and short-approach
vertical jump work outperformed straight sprint speed as a predictor.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
long jumpers, high jumpers, triple jumpers, and pole vaulters, both sexes. The "high jump
breaks the pattern" finding is specific to Bondarchuk's Soviet-era high jump technique
population (likely predominantly the Fosbury Flop or straddle technique of that era) and
should not be over-generalized without checking which technique his athletes used (not
stated in the excerpted pages). Applying any of these specific exercise priorities to a
football skill (e.g., a receiver's high-point jump) is Inference — no football population
data exists in this source.

**Example** — A long jump program prioritizing short-approach full-technique jumps (at
reduced run-up length) as the top assistance tool, alongside sprint work, is
well-supported by this data; the same prioritization for a high jumper should shift toward
short-approach vertical jumps and multi-jump work rather than assuming sprint speed
transfers the same way.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining why the short-run-up version outperforms more general exercises.
[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]] — the parallel finding for
sprinters using jump exercises as assistance work (the reverse direction of transfer).

# Barbell Snatch, Power Clean, Squat, and Bench Press All Transfer to Throwing — But Only Up to a Specific Result Level, Then Plateau

**What it is** — Across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer, Bondarchuk finds that all
four major strength exercises (snatch, power clean, squat with barbell on shoulders,
bench press — bench excluded for hammer throwers, who "do not use it") show a positive
transfer to the competitive throw, but **only up to a specific result level for each
exercise and event**, after which the correlation with further competitive improvement
disappears. Worked examples with locators: in discus, snatch transfer ended at 45-50m
(men) / 55-60m (women); power clean and squat ended at 50-55m; bench press extended
furthest, to 55-60m (men) / 65-70m (women). In hammer, snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean
65-70m, squat 60-65m; women's cumulative effect ran further, to 45-60m across all three.
In shot put, snatch ended at 17-18m (men)/15-16m (women), power clean at 14-15m
(men)/14-25m (women, likely an OCR artifact for a narrower band), squat at 19-20m
(men)/17-18m (women), bench at 18-19m (men)/19-20m (women). In javelin, snatch and power
clean both ended at 65-70m (men); squat showed no transfer at 50-55m; women's snatch ended
at 60-65m, power clean 50-55m, bench 45-50m, squat showed none at all. (PDF pp. 133-135,
printed pp. 116-118.) Bondarchuk's own aggregate summary across the whole book, at the
close of this chapter: "specialized-preparatory exercises have a positive influence on an
increase in the sports result in the basic event but up to a specific level of sports
mastery. Further on, they do not show a positive effect." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why the ceiling occurs at these specific
levels; **Inference:** this is consistent with a training-age/diminishing-returns pattern
common across strength and power sports — general strength qualities predict performance
strongly at lower levels of mastery, but as an athlete's absolute strength approaches the
level "required" for the skill, further strength gains stop being the limiting factor and
technical/specialized qualities (captured better by the specialized-developmental
exercises in [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]) take over as the
binding constraint. Bondarchuk does not state this diminishing-returns interpretation
himself in the excerpted text; it is this entry's own reading.

**When to apply** — Use as a rationale for shifting a throwing (or other power-sport)
athlete's programming emphasis away from general barbell strength work and toward
specialized-developmental work (implement-weight variation, technical throws) once the
athlete's absolute strength numbers cross into the "cumulative effect ends here" range for
their event, rather than continuing to chase strength PRs as the primary lever for
competitive improvement.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
throwers of both sexes, using a specific set of four lifts (Olympic-style snatch and power
clean, not necessarily modern variations; a barbell squat and bench press without stated
depth/technique standards). The exact result-level thresholds are specific to this
1970s-80s dataset and should not be treated as current standards. This entry does NOT mean
"stop lifting" once the ceiling is reached — see
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for the author's own
explicit statement that these exercises should still be used at reduced volume for
maintenance and restoration. Applying this ceiling-effect logic to a football strength
athlete (e.g., an offensive lineman) is Inference: no football population data exists
here, and a lineman's "competitive exercise" is far less discrete than a single measured
throw.

**Example** — A discus thrower already squatting well past the 50-55m-equivalent strength
level, per this data, should not expect further squat PRs alone to keep driving discus
distance; continued improvement is better targeted through implement-weight variation and
technical work (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), with
strength work maintained rather than chased.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] — the
specialized-developmental alternative that keeps transferring past this ceiling.
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] — what to do with
strength work once this ceiling is reached, in the author's own words.
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] — the parallel (and even more limited)
ceiling pattern for strength exercises in sprinting.

# Don't Cut a Strength Exercise Just Because It Stopped Predicting Further Competitive Improvement — Keep It at Lower Volume for Maintenance and Restoration

**What it is** — Having shown across sprints, jumps, and throws that specialized-
preparatory exercises (snatch, clean, squat, bench: see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
[[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]) stop predicting further competitive
improvement past a certain level of mastery, Bondarchuk draws an explicit practical
conclusion rather than leaving it as a pure data finding: "it does not mean that
specialized-preparatory exercises should be excluded from the training. In our view, it is
necessary to use them but to a somewhat lesser volume to maintain the achieved level, as
well as for carrying out restorative measures." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.) He goes
further, speculating that specialized-preparatory exercises may function as
"'stimulational factors' which on the brain level, create conditions for the transfer to
the main movement" even without producing measurable further gains themselves — a direct
echo of the "tie-in effect" idea from Chapter 1 (see
[[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]]). (PDF p. 175, printed
p. 158.)

**Why it works** — No new mechanism beyond the tie-in-effect hypothesis already flagged as
untested in Chapter 1; this is the author's own explicit hedge against a naive
misreading of his own ceiling-effect data (i.e., "the data shows no further correlation,
therefore cut the exercise" — which he directly warns against).

**When to apply** — Whenever a program uses Bondarchuk's own ceiling-effect findings (or
any similar correlation-based finding) to justify dropping a strength exercise once an
athlete's numbers plateau relative to competitive results, apply this counter-heuristic:
keep the exercise in the program at reduced volume for maintenance (residual strength
retention, consistent with the roughly-30-day residual training effect windows this
library already tracks — see `method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power") and for its
restorative/active-recovery role, rather than removing it outright.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own explicit
practical recommendation, offered as reasoned judgment built on his data rather than as a
separately tested finding in its own right — he flags his "stimulational factor" idea as
speculative ("it is very possible that... other methods... will be proposed"). Population
context is the same elite Soviet track and field throwers/sprinters/jumpers as the ceiling-
effect claims it responds to. Applying "keep it for maintenance, not for further gains" to
a football strength program's in-season lifting philosophy is Inference, though it is
directly consistent with Baylor's own stated in-season rule of "maintain intensity, reduce
volume" (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`) and its roughly-30-day strength residual
training effect window (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25`) — two independent sources converging on
the same practical conclusion (reduce, don't eliminate) even though they arrive at it from
different reasoning.

**Example** — A discus thrower whose squat numbers have plateaued relative to further
distance gains should keep squatting at a lower volume/frequency for strength maintenance
and recovery purposes, while shifting the primary developmental emphasis to implement-
weight variation (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), rather
than dropping squats from the program entirely.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]] and
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] — the data findings this heuristic is
a direct response to. [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]] —
the Chapter 1 idea (tie-in effect) this heuristic's "stimulational factor" speculation
echoes.

# The Barbell Snatch and Half Squat Transfer to Sprinting Only Up to a Narrow, Specific Performance Band, Then Stop

**What it is** — Tables 51-60 (PDF pp. 91-99, printed pp. 74-82) correlate the barbell
snatch and half squat (with barbell on shoulders) against 100m/200m/400m and hurdle
results across five to six performance bands per event. Bondarchuk's own reading: overall
interrelationship is poor, and where a positive ("cumulative") effect exists at all, it is
confined to specific, narrow bands rather than holding across all qualification levels.
Examples with locators: men's 100m snatch/squat "cumulative effect" only up to
11.10-11.40s (Table 51: snatch coefficients range from -0.186 at 10.20-10.50s up to only
0.396 at 11.10-11.40s); women's snatch shows an effect on only one band, 12.70-12.79s
(Table 56); in the 400m hurdles, "a positive interrelationship... was not seen" at all,
with correlation coefficients ranging only 0.196-0.320 (Table 55, printed p. 77, citing
his own summary sentence at PDF p. 89/printed p. 72). Throws of the shot forward/backward
were even weaker transfer exercises, positive only for 110m hurdlers at two narrow bands
(13.50-14.00s and 14.00-14.50s) and absent elsewhere. (PDF pp. 88-90, printed pp. 71-73.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: "the cumulative effect from strength
exercises will appear only when they are close to the competitive event according to the
biomechanical aspects and methodological parameters" (PDF p. 102, printed p. 85) — i.e.
the snatch and squat are specialized-preparatory (per
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]), sharing muscle groups with sprinting but
not its movement structure, velocity, or ground-contact regime, so per
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] they sit further from the competitive
event in the transfer chain than the running-based exercises in
[[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]]. He explicitly declines to
call this "ineffectiveness," instead suggesting the missing transfer could be a
methodological artifact (rep count, session compactness, intensity zones used) rather than
a fixed property of the exercises. (PDF p. 102, printed p. 85.)

**When to apply** — Use as historical caution against assuming barbell strength numbers
(snatch, squat) will keep predicting sprint improvement once an athlete passes a certain
performance level; per this data, once an athlete is already fast, further improvement in
these lifts stops tracking with further sprint improvement. This does not mean drop the
lifts (see [[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for
Bondarchuk's own prescription on that point) — it means stop expecting them to be the
driver of further sprint gains at that point.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite and sub-elite
Soviet-era sprinters/hurdlers, both sexes, tested with a specific barbell snatch and a
half-squat-with-barbell-on-shoulders (not a full back squat, front squat, or trap-bar
variant); the finding should not be assumed to hold for a different strength exercise
variation without its own data. This is track and field data; extending "barbell strength
work plateaus in its transfer to top-end speed past a certain level" to football speed
training is Inference, though it is broadly consistent with general S&C literature on
strength/speed transfer diminishing at higher training ages — that broader literature was
not cross-checked in this ingest.

**Example** — A high-level 100m sprinter already running 10.2-10.4s should not expect
squat or snatch PRs to reliably predict further 100m improvement, per this data; a
developing sprinter in the 11.0-11.5s range is more likely to still be inside the band
where this book's data shows a measurable (if still modest) positive relationship.

**Related** — [[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]] — the much
stronger transfer picture for running-based assistance work in the same event group.
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] — Bondarchuk's own
prescription for what to do once an exercise stops producing further transfer.

# Barbell Snatch, Power Clean, Squat, and Bench Press All Transfer to Throwing — But Only Up to a Specific Result Level, Then Plateau

**What it is** — Across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer, Bondarchuk finds that all
four major strength exercises (snatch, power clean, squat with barbell on shoulders,
bench press — bench excluded for hammer throwers, who "do not use it") show a positive
transfer to the competitive throw, but **only up to a specific result level for each
exercise and event**, after which the correlation with further competitive improvement
disappears. Worked examples with locators: in discus, snatch transfer ended at 45-50m
(men) / 55-60m (women); power clean and squat ended at 50-55m; bench press extended
furthest, to 55-60m (men) / 65-70m (women). In hammer, snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean
65-70m, squat 60-65m; women's cumulative effect ran further, to 45-60m across all three.
In shot put, snatch ended at 17-18m (men)/15-16m (women), power clean at 14-15m
(men)/14-25m (women, likely an OCR artifact for a narrower band), squat at 19-20m
(men)/17-18m (women), bench at 18-19m (men)/19-20m (women). In javelin, snatch and power
clean both ended at 65-70m (men); squat showed no transfer at 50-55m; women's snatch ended
at 60-65m, power clean 50-55m, bench 45-50m, squat showed none at all. (PDF pp. 133-135,
printed pp. 116-118.) Bondarchuk's own aggregate summary across the whole book, at the
close of this chapter: "specialized-preparatory exercises have a positive influence on an
increase in the sports result in the basic event but up to a specific level of sports
mastery. Further on, they do not show a positive effect." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why the ceiling occurs at these specific
levels; **Inference:** this is consistent with a training-age/diminishing-returns pattern
common across strength and power sports — general strength qualities predict performance
strongly at lower levels of mastery, but as an athlete's absolute strength approaches the
level "required" for the skill, further strength gains stop being the limiting factor and
technical/specialized qualities (captured better by the specialized-developmental
exercises in [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]) take over as the
binding constraint. Bondarchuk does not state this diminishing-returns interpretation
himself in the excerpted text; it is this entry's own reading.

**When to apply** — Use as a rationale for shifting a throwing (or other power-sport)
athlete's programming emphasis away from general barbell strength work and toward
specialized-developmental work (implement-weight variation, technical throws) once the
athlete's absolute strength numbers cross into the "cumulative effect ends here" range for
their event, rather than continuing to chase strength PRs as the primary lever for
competitive improvement.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
throwers of both sexes, using a specific set of four lifts (Olympic-style snatch and power
clean, not necessarily modern variations; a barbell squat and bench press without stated
depth/technique standards). The exact result-level thresholds are specific to this
1970s-80s dataset and should not be treated as current standards. This entry does NOT mean
"stop lifting" once the ceiling is reached — see
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for the author's own
explicit statement that these exercises should still be used at reduced volume for
maintenance and restoration. Applying this ceiling-effect logic to a football strength
athlete (e.g., an offensive lineman) is Inference: no football population data exists
here, and a lineman's "competitive exercise" is far less discrete than a single measured
throw.

**Example** — A discus thrower already squatting well past the 50-55m-equivalent strength
level, per this data, should not expect further squat PRs alone to keep driving discus
distance; continued improvement is better targeted through implement-weight variation and
technical work (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), with
strength work maintained rather than chased.

# Specialized-Developmental Runs (Flying 30m, Blocks 30-200m) Correlate Strongly with Sprint/Hurdle Competitive Results

**What it is** — Tables 41-50 (PDF pp. 78-87, printed pp. 61-70) report correlation
coefficients between competitive results and other specialized-developmental/competitive
run distances, for men's and women's 100m, 200m, 400m, 110m/400m hurdles (men) and
100m/400m hurdles (women), each split by "high level" vs. "low level" athlete
qualification (the table note: high-level in the numerator, low-level in the denominator
for these specific tables — Tables 41-50 only; see the reversed convention noted in
`_book.md` for the throws tables). Bondarchuk's own summary: "the coefficients of
correlation in most cases are in the range of 0.700-0.800" (PDF p. 87, printed p. 70).
Representative individual values pulled directly: 100m runners' 30m-flying-start-to-100m
correlation 0.678/0.778 (high/low, Table 41); 110m hurdlers' 110m-hurdles-to-60m-from-
blocks correlation as low as 0.420 at one qualification level (Table 44); 400m hurdlers'
400m-hurdles-to-600m correlation as high as 0.890 (Table 45).

**Why it works** — No mechanism beyond the transfer-chain logic in
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]]: these are all specialized-
developmental or competitive-class exercises per
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] (shorter/longer runs at or near race
intensity), sharing most of the sprint or hurdle event's biomechanics and energy-system
demands, so high shared-element overlap predicts the observed high correlation.

**When to apply** — Use as historical evidence that assistance runs at varied distances
(flying starts, sub-maximal and supra-maximal segment lengths) are a reliably transferable
training tool for sprint/hurdle athletes, supporting programs that use varied-distance
sprint work rather than only full-distance reps. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355's
linear-sprint testing already uses split-time interpretation by physical quality (0-10m
acceleration, 30-40m speed) rather than total time alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Speed
and sprint," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`) — this book's high
segment-to-total correlations support treating those splits as meaningfully diagnostic,
not just a total-time proxy.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite and sub-elite
Soviet-era male and female sprinters and hurdlers (refs implicit in the tables' athlete
qualification split; exact sample sizes are not given in the excerpted pages). The
correlations described are all between running-based specialized-developmental/
competitive exercises — this entry does NOT cover strength or jump-exercise transfer,
which is markedly weaker (see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]]). Applying these specific
coefficients to football skill-position speed training is Inference: football speed
development sits inside a team-sport context with far less training-time devoted purely
to sprinting than a specialized Soviet track program, so the magnitude of these
correlations should not be assumed to hold as-is.

**Example** — A 200m runner's training program built heavily around 150m and 300m
repeats at race-adjacent intensity is well-supported by this data (150m-to-200m and
300m-to-200m correlations were among the higher entries in Table 42), more so than a
program relying mainly on much shorter (30m) segments for that specific event.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification these
correlated exercises fall into. [[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] —
the much weaker transfer picture for non-running assistance exercises in the same event
group.

# Jump-from-a-Short-Run-Up Is the Single Most Transferable Assistance Exercise for Every Jump Event; High Jump Is the Outlier

**What it is** — Tables 61-68 (PDF pp. 104-112, printed pp. 87-95) correlate running,
jumping, and strength/throw exercises against long jump, high jump, triple jump, and pole
vault results, men and women. Across long jump, triple jump, and pole vault, **all**
running and jumping exercises showed a cumulative positive effect; the two throwing
exercises (shot forward/backward) showed essentially none. The single strongest, most
consistent exercise across event types was the **jump/vault with a short run-up**: long
jumpers' correlation to a short-approach jump ran as high as 0.890-0.967 (Tables 61-62);
triple jumpers' short-run-up triple jump ran 0.890-0.954 for men, 0.700-0.906 for women
(Table 65-66); pole vaulters' short-run-up vault ran 0.745-0.865 (Tables 67-68). **High
jump was the outlier**: the author states plainly that in men's and women's high jump,
"in all cases, a weak interrelationship between the test results was observed on the
0.400 level" for running exercises specifically — the informative exercise there was
instead the vertical jump with a short run-up (0.876-0.965) and, unusually for a jump
event, the 10-fold jump from place (0.876-0.965, Tables 63-64) rather than the sprint
times that predicted every other jump event well. Barbell snatch showed almost no
transfer anywhere in this section except isolated single-level effects; the half squat
with barbell transferred more consistently, especially for high jump and pole vault (all
levels for both sexes in those two events). (PDF pp. 104-113, printed pp. 87-96.)

**Why it works** — Per [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] and
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]], the short-run-up version of each
event's own competitive movement is itself a specialized-developmental exercise (repeats
the competitive action's parts under an altered, easier condition), so it sits closest to
the competitive event in the transfer chain — consistent with it outperforming
general-preparatory sprint and strength exercises across every jump event tested. High
jump's break from the sprint-correlated pattern of the other three jump events is not
explained mechanistically by the author; **Inference:** the high jump's approach and
takeoff (curved run, back-to-the-bar rotation) differs enough biomechanically from a
straight-line sprint that raw straight-ahead sprint speed may simply share fewer
"identical elements" with it than with long jump, triple jump, or pole vault approaches.

**When to apply** — When selecting assistance work for a jump-event athlete, this data
supports prioritizing a short-approach version of the competitive jump itself as the
highest-value transfer exercise, over generic sprint times or barbell strength numbers,
with the explicit exception of high jump, where multi-jump (10-fold) and short-approach
vertical jump work outperformed straight sprint speed as a predictor.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
long jumpers, high jumpers, triple jumpers, and pole vaulters, both sexes. The "high jump
breaks the pattern" finding is specific to Bondarchuk's Soviet-era high jump technique
population (likely predominantly the Fosbury Flop or straddle technique of that era) and
should not be over-generalized without checking which technique his athletes used (not
stated in the excerpted pages). Applying any of these specific exercise priorities to a
football skill (e.g., a receiver's high-point jump) is Inference — no football population
data exists in this source.

**Example** — A long jump program prioritizing short-approach full-technique jumps (at
reduced run-up length) as the top assistance tool, alongside sprint work, is
well-supported by this data; the same prioritization for a high jumper should shift toward
short-approach vertical jumps and multi-jump work rather than assuming sprint speed
transfers the same way.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining why the short-run-up version outperforms more general exercises.
[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]] — the parallel finding for
sprinters using jump exercises as assistance work (the reverse direction of transfer).

# Training Transfer Comes in Four Flavors: Positive, Negative, Neutral, and Indifferent

**What it is** — Bondarchuk names three standard types of training transfer plus a fourth
he flags as rarer and specific to high-level athletes (PDF pp. 31-32, printed pp. 14-15):
- **Positive**: an increase in one exercise's result parallels an increase in another.
- **Negative**: an increase in preparation for one exercise coincides with a decrease in
  another.
- **Neutral** (also "indifferent" in some literature he cites): no measurable effect
  either way.
- **Indifferent/double effect** (his own added category, "met more rarely," specifically
  in high-level athletes using a complex of different exercises): one exercise can help
  and hurt at the same time along different dimensions, e.g. heavier-implement throws
  positive for strength but negative for technique — "there is a noticeable worsening of
  technique in some throws with the use of heavier implements" (refs [18, 152]). Bondarchuk
  gives a specific example: race walkers doing high volumes of aerobic/anaerobic running in
  general preparation showed improved heart-circulatory/respiratory function but worsened
  walking technique (ref [94]), a case of positive-physiological/negative-technical
  double effect. (PDF p. 32, printed p. 15.)

**Why it works** — The positive/negative/neutral categorization itself is a long-standing,
independently established construct in the broader transfer-of-learning literature
(traced by the author himself to E.L. Thorndike's identical-elements theory, cited earlier
in Chapter 1) and is not unique to this book. **This entry keeps the book's `supported`
ceiling** because Bondarchuk's specific fourth category (double/indifferent effect) and
his worked examples are his own, uncross-checked additions, not independently verified
findings. **Inference:** the "double effect" category is a useful naming for something
coaches see constantly (an exercise that builds capacity while degrading movement
quality) but that most popular S&C literature collapses into a vague "watch the technique
cost" warning rather than naming as its own transfer category.

**When to apply** — Use the four-way split as a checklist when introducing a new
exercise: is the expected effect positive, negative, neutral, or a **double effect**
where it will help one quality while hurting another (most often physical capacity up,
technique down, from overloaded implements/loads)? The walking example is the clean
illustration — flag any high-volume general-conditioning block for a technical,
timing-sensitive sport skill (sprinting, throwing, agility) as a double-effect risk, not
just a "general conditioning is fine" default.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The category examples given (heavier
implements degrading throw technique, aerobic-volume race walkers losing walking
technique) are drawn from Soviet-era track and field research cited only by bracketed
reference number [18, 94, 152], not verified against the original sources in this ingest.
Population is elite track and field throwers and race walkers; extending "double effect"
reasoning to football (e.g., heavy sled work degrading sprint mechanics) is Inference,
plausible by analogy but not something this passage tests.

**Example** — **Inference:** a college lineman doing high-volume heavy sled pushes for
GPP strength may show a positive effect on force production and a negative (double)
effect on start technique and shin angle if the sled load or volume is not periodically
reduced back toward the competitive movement pattern, echoing the walker's aerobic-volume
example here.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining,
staging) — the mechanism this claim's negative-transfer cases plausibly run through
(mismatch on one of the ten specificity dimensions).

# The Barbell Snatch and Half Squat Transfer to Sprinting Only Up to a Narrow, Specific Performance Band, Then Stop

**What it is** — Tables 51-60 (PDF pp. 91-99, printed pp. 74-82) correlate the barbell
snatch and half squat (with barbell on shoulders) against 100m/200m/400m and hurdle
results across five to six performance bands per event. Bondarchuk's own reading: overall
interrelationship is poor, and where a positive ("cumulative") effect exists at all, it is
confined to specific, narrow bands rather than holding across all qualification levels.
Examples with locators: men's 100m snatch/squat "cumulative effect" only up to
11.10-11.40s (Table 51: snatch coefficients range from -0.186 at 10.20-10.50s up to only
0.396 at 11.10-11.40s); women's snatch shows an effect on only one band, 12.70-12.79s
(Table 56); in the 400m hurdles, "a positive interrelationship... was not seen" at all,
with correlation coefficients ranging only 0.196-0.320 (Table 55 itself at PDF p. 95,
printed p. 78; the "not seen" summary sentence and the 0.196-0.320 range are Bondarchuk's
own text at PDF p. 89, printed p. 72). Throws of the shot forward/backward
were even weaker transfer exercises, positive only for 110m hurdlers at two narrow bands
(13.50-14.00s and 14.00-14.50s) and absent elsewhere. (PDF pp. 88-90, printed pp. 71-73.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: "the cumulative effect from strength
exercises will appear only when they are close to the competitive event according to the
biomechanical aspects and methodological parameters" (PDF p. 102, printed p. 85) — i.e.
the snatch and squat are specialized-preparatory (per
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]), sharing muscle groups with sprinting but
not its movement structure, velocity, or ground-contact regime, so per
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] they sit further from the competitive
event in the transfer chain than the running-based exercises in
[[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]]. He explicitly declines to
call this "ineffectiveness," instead suggesting the missing transfer could be a
methodological artifact (rep count, session compactness, intensity zones used) rather than
a fixed property of the exercises. (PDF p. 102, printed p. 85.)

**When to apply** — Use as historical caution against assuming barbell strength numbers
(snatch, squat) will keep predicting sprint improvement once an athlete passes a certain
performance level; per this data, once an athlete is already fast, further improvement in
these lifts stops tracking with further sprint improvement. This does not mean drop the
lifts (see [[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for
Bondarchuk's own prescription on that point) — it means stop expecting them to be the
driver of further sprint gains at that point.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite and sub-elite
Soviet-era sprinters/hurdlers, both sexes, tested with a specific barbell snatch and a
half-squat-with-barbell-on-shoulders (not a full back squat, front squat, or trap-bar
variant); the finding should not be assumed to hold for a different strength exercise
variation without its own data. This is track and field data; extending "barbell strength
work plateaus in its transfer to top-end speed past a certain level" to football speed
training is Inference, though it is broadly consistent with general S&C literature on
strength/speed transfer diminishing at higher training ages — that broader literature was
not cross-checked in this ingest.

**Example** — A high-level 100m sprinter already running 10.2-10.4s should not expect
squat or snatch PRs to reliably predict further 100m improvement, per this data; a
developing sprinter in the 11.0-11.5s range is more likely to still be inside the band
where this book's data shows a measurable (if still modest) positive relationship.

**Related** — [[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]] — the much
stronger transfer picture for running-based assistance work in the same event group.
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] — Bondarchuk's own
prescription for what to do once an exercise stops producing further transfer.

# Among Assistance Exercises, Multi-Jump Work (Ten-Fold Jump, Leg-to-Leg Bounds) Transfers to Sprinting Most Consistently — More Than Single Jumps, Throws, or Barbell Lifts

**What it is** — Comparing all the specialized-preparatory assistance exercises tested
against sprint/hurdle competitive results (barbell snatch, half squat, standing long jump,
vertical jump, triple jump from place, 10-fold jump from place, leg-to-leg jumps for 50m,
forward/backward shot throws), Bondarchuk identifies the **10-fold jump from place** and
**leg-to-leg (bounding) jumps for 50m** as "more transferable than other specialized-
preparatory exercises," measured not by having the single highest correlation coefficient
but by the number of qualification-level bands across which a positive cumulative effect
appears (PDF p. 99, printed p. 82). Concretely: leg-to-leg jumps for 50m showed a
cumulative effect on **all levels** for both men's and women's 100m, and across the full
range for women's 100m hurdles (12.80-15.80s) and men's 400m hurdles (49.50-55.50s) (PDF
p. 100, printed p. 83). By contrast, the standing long jump, vertical jump, and triple
jump from place each showed positive transfer only on two-to-three of five levels for most
events, and high jump/pole vault-style single jumps were even more level-restricted for
sprint events specifically (not their own competitive event). He generalizes: "with an
increase in a number of take-offs when executing the above mentioned jump exercises, there
is an increase in the number of cases of positive transfer" — proposing multi-jump
exercises over long ground-contact segments (20-150m) as the most broadly transferable
jump category for track and field generally. (PDF pp. 100-101, printed pp. 83-84.)

**Why it works** — His own stated mechanism: multi-jump exercises over distance "repeat
the biomechanical parameters of the competitive movement" more closely than single jumps,
"have a similar appearance to the muscle work regimes, and use the same intensity zones,"
and can duplicate the sprint's actual duration/segment structure (e.g. matching a starting-
acceleration segment specifically). (PDF p. 101, printed p. 84.) In the terms of
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], repeated bounding over a real sprint-
relevant distance sits closer to specialized-developmental than a single standing jump
does, which under [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] predicts exactly
the stronger, more level-consistent transfer observed here.

**When to apply** — When choosing between plyometric/jump exercise variants for a
sprint-focused program, this data favors prioritizing repeated multi-jump/bounding work
over set distances (matched to the target phase of the sprint — acceleration vs. max
velocity) over single-effort jumps (standing long jump, vertical jump) as the more
consistently transferable choice, while still using single jumps for their own
diagnostic/training value.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
sprinters and hurdlers, both sexes; "leg-to-leg jumps for 50m" and "10-fold jump from
place" are specific, defined tests in this text, not a stand-in for every modern bounding
or plyometric variation. The claim is about *transfer consistency across qualification
levels*, not about which exercise has the single highest correlation value — do not
conflate the two when citing this entry. Applying this preference (multi-jump over
single-jump assistance work) to football speed/power training is Inference, plausible by
analogy to established plyometric literature but not tested here on a football
population.

**Example** — A sprint-development block choosing between a session of standing long
jumps and a session of 10-15 continuous alternate-leg bounds over 30-50m would, per this
data, expect the bounding session to transfer more reliably across a wider range of athlete
ability levels.

**Related** — [[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]] — the
running-based exercises that transfer even more strongly than jumps in this event group.
[[claim--jump-event-exercise-transfer-patterns]] — the parallel (and partly consistent)
finding for jump-event athletes' own competitive results.

# The Longer the Competitive Distance, the Wider the Range of Segment Distances That Transfer to It — Except at the Ultra-Endurance Extreme

**What it is** — Tables 89-103 (PDF pp. 149-160, printed pp. 132-143) correlate training
segment distances (60m to marathon/50km) against competitive results in the 800m through
marathon and 10/20/50km race walks. Bondarchuk's own summary pattern: "with an increase
in the distance, transfer of physical abilities begins with the longer segments" — 800m
and 1500m runners show a cumulative effect starting as short as the 60m segment; men's
steeplechase and women's 3000m start from 600m and 400m respectively; 5000m runners' range
starts around 600m; marathoners' range starts at 5000m (men) or 3000m (women) — i.e., the
*shortest* segment that still transfers gets longer as the competitive event itself gets
longer. (PDF pp. 160-161, printed pp. 143-144.) Representative correlation values: men's
800m showed its strongest correlations with the 400m, 600m, and 1000m segments (0.700-0.912,
Table 89), with a sharp drop by the 1500m and further by 3000-5000m; women's 3000m showed
positive transfer across every tested segment, strongest with 1000m/1500m/5000m
(0.725-0.906, Table 99). At the ultra-endurance extreme, the pattern breaks: marathoners
(and 10km-walk women / 50km-walk men) show **no** cumulative effect from segments *longer*
than the competitive distance, "because in sports practice similar tests do not exist" —
there is nothing longer to test against. (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144.) Race-walkers'
running-distance correlations (5000m/10000m run vs. walk results) were uniformly weak
(0.354-0.400), far below their same-discipline walk-distance correlations (up to 0.800+).
(PDF pp. 148-149, printed pp. 131-132.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk attributes the general pattern to "the specifics of the
interaction of systems involved in the training effect" — different aerobic/anaerobic-
alactate/anaerobic-lactate energy-system demands at different distances (general systemic
reactions) plus the individual athlete's short- and long-term adaptational responses
(specific reactions). (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144.) He does not fully resolve *why* the
transfer range widens with distance beyond this general systems-interaction language.
**Inference:** the pattern is consistent with the widely-established idea that longer
events draw on a broader mix of energy systems and pacing demands, so a wider band of
training distances can stress a physiologically relevant system for that event; this
broader interpretation is this entry's own reading, not stated by the author.

**When to apply** — Use as historical support for distance-specific training range
selection: shorter competitive events (800m-1500m) can be trained effectively with a
narrower, shorter set of segment distances; longer events (5000m-marathon) benefit from
(and require) a wider spread of training distances, from well below race distance up to
race distance itself, to cover the full transfer range this data shows. **Eric's
baseline:** HHPR 5355 already treats aerobic-system training for speed-power athletes as
mainly serving inter-effort recovery rather than distance capacity, kept below anaerobic
threshold at roughly a 1:1-1:2 work:rest ratio (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and
energy systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.51`) — this book's population is exclusively
dedicated distance-event specialists, a very different training context from a
speed-power athlete's incidental aerobic work, so this entry's distance-range findings
should not be imported into football conditioning design without that distinction in mind.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
middle/long/ultra-distance runners and race walkers, both sexes; the specific segment
distances and correlation values are dataset-specific. This entry covers **running/walking
segment distances only** — it says nothing about strength, jump, or throw-exercise
transfer to endurance events (not tested in this chapter). Applying "wider transfer range
for longer events" to a team-sport repeated-sprint or intermittent-endurance context
(football's actual endurance demand, per `method-baseline.md`'s energy-systems framing) is
Inference: football conditioning is not a single continuous-distance competitive event in
the way every sport in this dataset is.

**Example** — A 10,000m runner's program using training distances from 600m intervals up
to marathon-length long runs is well-supported by this data's transfer-range findings; a
marathoner's program should not expect any additional transfer benefit from segments
longer than the marathon itself, since no such segment exists to test or train.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — general classification
these segment distances fall under (specialized-developmental to competitive, depending on
how close the segment is to full race distance).

# Bondarchuk's Own Four Exercise Classes, in His Own Words: General Preparatory, Specialized-Preparatory, Specialized-Developmental, Competitive

**What it is** — This is the primary-source definition of the classification this book's
own title concept depends on, drawn from Bondarchuk's Glossary (not from Chapter 2's
prose, which assumes the reader already knows these terms):
- **General (Preparatory) Exercises / GPP**: "do not repeat the competitive actions as a
  whole or their separate parts. Other muscle groups take part in the work being done. The
  functional systems of the body are activated but do not ensure an increase in results in
  the competitive exercise." Function: all-round development, work capacity, and active
  rest/restoration. (PDF p. 12, printed p. x.)
- **Specialized-Preparatory Exercises / SPP**: like general exercises, "do not repeat the
  competitive actions as a whole or in their separate parts. However, they use similar
  muscle groups in their execution," activating the functions and body systems the main
  movement depends on, with "identical or close to identical regimes of muscle work."
  (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Specialized-Developmental Exercises / SDE**: "repeat the competitive exercise in its
  separate parts. In executing them, one and the same muscle groups participate, together
  with activation of similar systems and organs. They not only repeat the muscle work
  regime and other systems of the body... but also supersede them," and "serve for entry
  into the state of sports form." (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Competitive Exercises / CE**: "the acting definition... is 'sport event,' in which the
  athlete participates in competition," executed either in actual competition or in
  training as a model/repeat of competitive conditions, easier or harder. (PDF p. 12,
  printed p. x-xi.)
Chapter 2's own intro adds a cross-cutting distinction independent of the four classes: a
**local** exercise (uses separate parts/body links — squat, bench press, standing long
jump, vertical jump) versus a **global** exercise (uses all body links together — the
barbell clean). (PDF p. 75, printed p. 58.)

**Why it works** — The four classes form an ordered continuum of how much of the
competitive movement (muscle groups, movement structure, muscle-work regime) an exercise
reproduces, which is the same logic underlying
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and the specifist "identical
elements" position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]: more shared
elements with the competitive movement should predict more reliable positive transfer.
Chapter 2's correlational data (see the claim entries below) is this book's attempt to
test that prediction empirically, event by event.

**When to apply** — Use as the primary-source definition when auditing any exercise
selection against this taxonomy, in place of or alongside secondary paraphrases of it.
**Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in HHPR 5355 is taught "on a spectrum from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of 'sport specific'"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`; `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`) — this entry
gives that course material its primary-source citation and exact definitions. This
library already has a secondary-source treatment of the same taxonomy in
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault), built from Moyer's course paraphrase rather than Bondarchuk's own text; that
entry's table ("GPE/SPE/SDE/CE") matches this one closely but labels Moyer's own sprint
examples (bounding, banded pawback, etc.), not Bondarchuk's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, not proven: this is Bondarchuk's own
classification scheme, widely adopted in the Soviet/Russian sport-science tradition and
cross-referenced by Verkhoshansky's circle (see the Related links), but it is a
practitioner taxonomy, not an independently tested causal model, and the boundary between
classes is fuzzy in application (the Moyer-derived entry below makes the same point about
sprint exercises specifically). The four-class definitions here are written for individual
track and field events; a football skill (e.g., a pass rush) is a much less discrete,
single "competitive exercise" than a 100m sprint or a hammer throw, so classifying a given
drill as SPP vs. SDE for football is Inference, not something Bondarchuk's glossary
addresses.

**Example** — For a shot putter: general preparatory = general conditioning running;
specialized-preparatory = barbell snatch, half squat (same leg-extensor muscle groups,
different movement); specialized-developmental = throwing a lighter or heavier shot
(repeats the throw's parts under altered load); competitive = throwing the 7.26kg
competition shot in a meet.

**Related** — `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault) — the secondary, Moyer-course paraphrase of this same taxonomy; **reciprocal-link
suggestion**: add a note there pointing back to this primary-source entry once this book
clears the review gate. [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — the transfer
logic built on this classification. [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] —
the specifist theory this classification operationalizes.

# Bondarchuk's Own Four Exercise Classes, in His Own Words: General Preparatory, Specialized-Preparatory, Specialized-Developmental, Competitive

**What it is** — This is the primary-source definition of the classification this book's
own title concept depends on, drawn from Bondarchuk's Glossary (not from Chapter 2's
prose, which assumes the reader already knows these terms):
- **General (Preparatory) Exercises / GPP**: "do not repeat the competitive actions as a
  whole or their separate parts. Other muscle groups take part in the work being done. The
  functional systems of the body are activated but do not ensure an increase in results in
  the competitive exercise." Function: all-round development, work capacity, and active
  rest/restoration. (PDF p. 12, printed p. x.)
- **Specialized-Preparatory Exercises / SPP**: like general exercises, "do not repeat the
  competitive actions as a whole or in their separate parts. However, they use similar
  muscle groups in their execution," activating the functions and body systems the main
  movement depends on, with "identical or close to identical regimes of muscle work."
  (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Specialized-Developmental Exercises / SDE**: "repeat the competitive exercise in its
  separate parts. In executing them, one and the same muscle groups participate, together
  with activation of similar systems and organs. They not only repeat the muscle work
  regime and other systems of the body... but also supersede them," and "serve for entry
  into the state of sports form." (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Competitive Exercises / CE**: "the acting definition... is 'sport event,' in which the
  athlete participates in competition," executed either in actual competition or in
  training as a model/repeat of competitive conditions, easier or harder. (PDF p. 12,
  printed p. x-xi.)
Chapter 2's own intro adds a cross-cutting distinction independent of the four classes: a
**local** exercise (uses separate parts/body links — squat, bench press, standing long
jump, vertical jump) versus a **global** exercise (uses all body links together — the
barbell clean). (PDF p. 75, printed p. 58.)

**Why it works** — The four classes form an ordered continuum of how much of the
competitive movement (muscle groups, movement structure, muscle-work regime) an exercise
reproduces, which is the same logic underlying
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and the specifist "identical
elements" position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]: more shared
elements with the competitive movement should predict more reliable positive transfer.
Chapter 2's correlational data (see the claim entries below) is this book's attempt to
test that prediction empirically, event by event.

**When to apply** — Use as the primary-source definition when auditing any exercise
selection against this taxonomy, in place of or alongside secondary paraphrases of it.
**Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in HHPR 5355 is taught "on a spectrum from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of 'sport specific'"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`; `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`) — this entry
gives that course material its primary-source citation and exact definitions. This
library already has a secondary-source treatment of the same taxonomy in
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault), built from Moyer's course paraphrase rather than Bondarchuk's own text; that
entry's table ("GPE/SPE/SDE/CE") matches this one closely but labels Moyer's own sprint
examples (bounding, banded pawback, etc.), not Bondarchuk's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, not proven: this is Bondarchuk's own
classification scheme. Two other sources in this library already use it independently
(the `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer` vault entry linked above, and Eric's HHPR 5355
course per `method-baseline.md`), which is evidence the taxonomy circulated beyond this
one book, but this ingest did not check how far it spread through the wider Soviet/Russian
sport-science literature, so that broader claim is not made here. It is a practitioner
taxonomy, not an independently tested causal model, and the boundary between
classes is fuzzy in application (the Moyer-derived entry below makes the same point about
sprint exercises specifically). The four-class definitions here are written for individual
track and field events; a football skill (e.g., a pass rush) is a much less discrete,
single "competitive exercise" than a 100m sprint or a hammer throw, so classifying a given
drill as SPP vs. SDE for football is Inference, not something Bondarchuk's glossary
addresses.

**Example** — For a shot putter: general preparatory = general conditioning running;
specialized-preparatory = barbell snatch, half squat (same leg-extensor muscle groups,
different movement); specialized-developmental = throwing a lighter or heavier shot
(repeats the throw's parts under altered load); competitive = throwing the 7.26kg
competition shot in a meet.

**Related** — `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault) — the secondary, Moyer-course paraphrase of this same taxonomy; **reciprocal-link
suggestion**: add a note there pointing back to this primary-source entry once this book
clears the review gate. [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — the transfer
logic built on this classification. [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] —
the specifist theory this classification operationalizes.

jump, vertical jump) versus a **global** exercise (uses all body links together — the
barbell clean). (PDF p. 75, printed p. 58.)

**Why it works** — The four classes form an ordered continuum of how much of the
competitive movement (muscle groups, movement structure, muscle-work regime) an exercise
reproduces, which is the same logic underlying
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and the specifist "identical
elements" position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]: more shared
elements with the competitive movement should predict more reliable positive transfer.
Chapter 2's correlational data (see the claim entries below) is this book's attempt to
test that prediction empirically, event by event.

**When to apply** — Use as the primary-source definition when auditing any exercise
selection against this taxonomy, in place of or alongside secondary paraphrases of it.
**Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in HHPR 5355 is taught "on a spectrum from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of 'sport specific'"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`; `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`) — this entry
gives that course material its primary-source citation and exact definitions. This
library already has a secondary-source treatment of the same taxonomy in
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault), built from Moyer's course paraphrase rather than Bondarchuk's own text; that
entry's table ("GPE/SPE/SDE/CE") matches this one closely but labels Moyer's own sprint
examples (bounding, banded pawback, etc.), not Bondarchuk's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, not proven: this is Bondarchuk's own
classification scheme. Two other sources in this library already use it independently
(the `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer` vault entry linked above, and Eric's HHPR 5355
course per `method-baseline.md`), which is evidence the taxonomy circulated beyond this
one book, but this ingest did not check how far it spread through the wider Soviet/Russian
sport-science literature, so that broader claim is not made here. It is a practitioner
taxonomy, not an independently tested causal model, and the boundary between
classes is fuzzy in application (the Moyer-derived entry below makes the same point about
sprint exercises specifically). The four-class definitions here are written for individual
track and field events; a football skill (e.g., a pass rush) is a much less discrete,
single "competitive exercise" than a 100m sprint or a hammer throw, so classifying a given
drill as SPP vs. SDE for football is Inference, not something Bondarchuk's glossary
addresses.

**Example** — For a shot putter: general preparatory = general conditioning running;
specialized-preparatory = barbell snatch, half squat (same leg-extensor muscle groups,
different movement); specialized-developmental = throwing a lighter or heavier shot
(repeats the throw's parts under altered load); competitive = throwing the 7.26kg
competition shot in a meet.

**Related** — `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`

anaerobic training loads.  In our discussions we will compare the most frequently used
