# Aerobic-to-Anaerobic-Alactate Transfer Is Broad and One-Directional; Anaerobic-Alactate-to-Aerobic Transfer Is Almost Absent

**What it is** — Tables 104-109 (PDF pp. 166-171, printed pp. 149-154) report, for pairs
of energy-system training loads (aerobic, anaerobic-alactate, anaerobic-lactate), how many
of a set of physiological indices (heart rate, respiratory rate, lung ventilation, oxygen
reserve/debt, VO2max, blood lactate, energy expenditure/source, muscle fiber type, and
effect on time-to-sports-form) are "fully transferred," "frequently transferred," or
"non-transferred" from one training-load type to the other. The pattern is asymmetric, not
mutual, between each pair:
- **Aerobic → anaerobic-alactate**: mostly transferable — Bondarchuk states "6 of 7" of
  the cardiovascular/respiratory functional indices are "fully transferable" (Table 104,
  PDF p. 162, printed p. 145). Non-transferable factors are specifically blood-lactate
  level and most energy-formation/energy-source factors, consistent with different
  fiber-type recruitment (red/slow fibers in aerobic work vs. white/fast fibers in
  anaerobic-alactate work, per the table's own row).
- **Aerobic ↔ anaerobic-lactate**: broadly transferable both ways — "of the 16 tests
  looked at, only four were non-transferable" (Table 105, PDF p. 163, printed p. 146); the
  anaerobic-lactate load actually *shortens* the time to enter sports form in aerobic
  training, while aerobic training does not shorten anaerobic-lactate's timeline (PDF pp.
  163-165, 171, printed pp. 146-148, 154).
- **Anaerobic-alactate → aerobic**: almost no transfer — "non-transferable factors here
  are all the remaining factors — 13 out of 15" (Table 108, PDF p. 164, printed p. 147),
  attributed to the oxygen-deficient conditions anaerobic-alactate work requires versus
  the oxygen-dependent structure of aerobic work.
- **Anaerobic-lactate → anaerobic-alactate**: also limited, though the reverse direction
  (anaerobic-lactate loads shorten anaerobic-alactate's time to sports form, but not vice
  versa) shows a similar one-way asymmetry to the aerobic/anaerobic-lactate pair (Tables
  106-107, PDF pp. 164, 169, printed pp. 147, 152).
Bondarchuk names a single-athlete example of the practical upshot of well-combined
aerobic/anaerobic training: "S. Auita" (almost certainly Saïd Aouita, transliterated) held
world records simultaneously across the 1500m, 5000m, and 2-mile distances, was within
tenths of a second of record pace at 2000m/3000m/1 mile, and is listed with additional
career bests: 200m-22.8, 400m-46.9, 1000m-2:15.16, steeplechase-8:21.92, 10,000m-27:26.11.
(PDF p. 172, printed p. 155.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own stated explanation is fiber-type recruitment: aerobic
training loads primarily adapt red (slow-twitch) fibers, while anaerobic-alactate and
anaerobic-lactate loads primarily adapt white (fast-twitch) fibers, and he states plainly
for at least one asymmetry that "it is not known why" one direction shortens
time-to-sports-form and the other does not (PDF p. 164, printed p. 147) — the author
himself flags this as an open question, not a resolved mechanism. Do not read a fuller
physiological explanation into this than the fiber-type note the text actually gives.

**When to apply** — Use this asymmetry as a caution against assuming energy-system
training transfers symmetrically: a block of aerobic work may build a genuine base for
anaerobic-alactate and anaerobic-lactate capacity (per the "fully transferred" majority in
Tables 104-105), but a block of anaerobic-alactate (pure sprint/power) work should **not**
be expected to build aerobic capacity — per this data it does not, on all but 2 of 15
tracked physiological indices. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches that all
three energy systems are always active simultaneously and that programming should target
the intended adaptation rather than the drill label (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning
and energy systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.19`; `class-4-2026.md p.15`) — this
entry's asymmetry finding sharpens that general principle into a specific, one-directional
claim about which energy-system work can substitute for which.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported** for the aggregate Tables 104-109
findings (described as "collective data" in each table's own title, i.e. pooled across
Bondarchuk's tested athletes, sample size not stated in the excerpted pages).
**Confidence is untested for the S. Auita/Aouita example**, a single named-athlete case
offered as illustration, not independent evidence. The tested population is elite Soviet
and international middle/long-distance track athletes; the specific physiological index
values (e.g. lactic acid concentrations, VO2 figures) are dataset-specific and should not
be treated as current normative standards. Applying this energy-system transfer asymmetry
directly to football conditioning (a repeated-sprint, intermittent-effort sport rather than
a continuous single-energy-system event) is Inference — no football or team-sport
population appears anywhere in this book.

**Example** — A program that substitutes heavy sprint/power ("anaerobic-alactate")
conditioning for aerobic base work, expecting it to also build aerobic capacity, is not
supported by this data: per Table 108, 13 of 15 tracked indices showed no transfer in that
direction. The reverse substitution (using aerobic work to partially support
anaerobic-alactate capacity) has much more support in this data (Table 104).

**Related** — No existing library entry addresses this specific aerobic/anaerobic transfer
asymmetry; cross-reference with `method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems,"
for Eric's own energy-system programming framework, and with
[[claim--endurance-event-transfer-range-widens-with-distance]] for the companion finding
on how far training segment distances (rather than energy-system type) transfer within a
single distance-running event.

**Extractor bug found and swept for during this batch:** `extract_pdf.py --pages A-B` is
end-exclusive — it returns pages A through B-1, silently dropping the requested last page.
Every extraction call in this batch was cross-checked against this behavior: for each
`A-B` request, the actual returned range is `A` to `B-1`, and the next call in the
sequence was confirmed to start at or before the dropped page so no page was skipped
between two calls. Two real content gaps were found and fixed:
1. PDF pages 162-173 (printed 145-156) were missed not because of the extractor bug but
   because two intermediate `head -c` / `tail -c` shell truncations (used to keep raw text
   out of the working context) cut the middle out of a wider request. Re-fetched in full;
   the content (Tables 104-109, the aerobic/anaerobic-alactate/anaerobic-lactate transfer
   matrix, and the S. Auita/Aouita multi-distance example) is now
   `claim--aerobic-anaerobic-energy-system-transfer-asymmetry.md`.
2. PDF pages 52-65 (printed 35-48, more of the Model Characteristics tables, 15-34) were
   intentionally skipped, not lost to the bug — confirmed by a follow-up probe that this
   range is pure normative tables, no narrative prose, consistent with
   `claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification.md`'s existing disclosure
   that not all 34 tables were transcribed.

# Two Test Families: "General" Tests Shared Across Events, "Specialized" Tests Unique to Each

**What it is** — Bondarchuk splits the tests used to study training transfer into two
families (PDF pp. 68-69, printed pp. 51-52):
- **General tests**: not tests of general-preparatory exercises specifically, but tests
  "used in mixed groups or between groups" — i.e., shared across many events. For
  heart-circulatory/respiratory function, nearly identical tests are used across all of
  track and field (max oxygen uptake on a veloergometer, time-to-exhaustion at max VO2,
  anaerobic threshold). For speed-strength sports, common general tests are the 60m run
  from blocks, barbell snatch, half squat with barbell, standing long jump, vertical jump
  (Abalakov method), triple jump from place, and forward/backward shot throws.
- **Specialized tests**: tests unique to each event's specific demands, most reliably
  results in **specialized-developmental exercises** — i.e., the competitive movement
  itself executed under lighter or more difficult conditions (lighter/heavier implements
  in throws, shorter approach runs in jumps, varied segment/rest combinations in cyclical
  events). He states specialized-developmental test reliability is the best-established
  of the test types; general-preparatory and specialized-preparatory test reliability is
  explicitly flagged as "not fully confirmed" and something to be "tightened up in the
  near future." (PDF p. 69, printed p. 52.)

**Why it works** — The logic follows directly from
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]]: since specialized-developmental
exercises sit closest to the competitive event in the transfer chain, tests built from
those same exercises should track competitive readiness more reliably than tests built
from more general exercises further from the competitive movement.

**When to apply** — When designing or auditing a testing battery, prioritize tests that
are themselves specialized-developmental-class movements (the competitive skill under
altered load/distance conditions) over generic strength/power tests when the goal is
tracking competitive readiness specifically; reserve the generic tests (snatch, squat,
vertical jump, etc.) for tracking general physical qualities, which the author himself
says have less-confirmed reliability as *transfer* indicators even though they are
common practice.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own
methodological framing for the correlational study that follows in Chapter 2, presented
without a formal reliability study of his own two test families in the excerpted pages
(he cites "already been shown" reliability for specialized-developmental tests, but gives
no reference number here). Population is Soviet track and field testing practice of the
1970s-80s; the specific listed general tests (barbell snatch, Abalakov jump, etc.) reflect
that era's tools, not necessarily current force-plate/GPS-based options. Applying the
general/specialized test distinction to Baylor's own battery design (`method-baseline.md`,
"Testing and assessment") is Inference in terms of which specific tests to pick, though
the underlying logic (prefer tests closest to the competitive movement for readiness
tracking) is directly portable.

**Example** — For a football wide receiver, a "specialized" test in this framework would
be a competitive-adjacent movement under altered conditions (e.g., a route run against a
lighter or heavier resistance band, or a shortened-approach vertical jump), while a
"general" test would be a standard vertical jump or broad jump shared across every
position group.

**Related** — [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — the transfer logic
this test-selection framework is built on.

# Specialized-Developmental Runs (Flying 30m, Blocks 30-200m) Correlate Strongly with Sprint/Hurdle Competitive Results

**What it is** — Tables 41-50 (PDF pp. 78-87, printed pp. 61-70) report correlation
coefficients between competitive results and other specialized-developmental/competitive
run distances, for men's and women's 100m, 200m, 400m, 110m/400m hurdles (men) and
100m/400m hurdles (women), each split by "high level" vs. "low level" athlete
qualification (the table note: high-level in the numerator, low-level in the denominator
for these specific tables — Tables 41-50 only; see the reversed convention noted in
`_book.md` for the throws tables). Bondarchuk's own summary: "the coefficients of
correlation in most cases are in the range of 0.700-0.800" (PDF p. 87, printed p. 70).
Representative individual values pulled directly (high-qualification/low-qualification):
100m runners' 30m-flying-start correlated 0.678/0.778 with the 30m-from-blocks segment and
0.756/0.876 with the 100m-from-blocks segment (Table 41); 110m hurdlers' 110m-hurdles
result correlated only 0.562/0.420 with the 200m-from-blocks segment, the weakest pairing
in that table (Table 44); 400m hurdlers' 400m-hurdles result correlated as high as
0.890/0.806 with the 600m-from-a-high-start segment (Table 45).

**Why it works** — No mechanism beyond the transfer-chain logic in
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]]: these are all specialized-
developmental or competitive-class exercises per
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] (shorter/longer runs at or near race
intensity), sharing most of the sprint or hurdle event's biomechanics and energy-system
demands, so high shared-element overlap predicts the observed high correlation.

**When to apply** — Use as historical evidence that assistance runs at varied distances
(flying starts, sub-maximal and supra-maximal segment lengths) are a reliably transferable
training tool for sprint/hurdle athletes, supporting programs that use varied-distance
sprint work rather than only full-distance reps. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355's
linear-sprint testing already uses split-time interpretation by physical quality (0-10m
acceleration, 30-40m speed) rather than total time alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Speed
and sprint," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`) — this book's high
segment-to-total correlations support treating those splits as meaningfully diagnostic,
not just a total-time proxy.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite and sub-elite
Soviet-era male and female sprinters and hurdlers (refs implicit in the tables' athlete
qualification split; exact sample sizes are not given in the excerpted pages). The
correlations described are all between running-based specialized-developmental/
competitive exercises — this entry does NOT cover strength or jump-exercise transfer,
which is markedly weaker (see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]]). Applying these specific
coefficients to football skill-position speed training is Inference: football speed
development sits inside a team-sport context with far less training-time devoted purely
to sprinting than a specialized Soviet track program, so the magnitude of these
correlations should not be assumed to hold as-is.

**Example** — A 200m runner's training program built heavily around 150m and 300m
repeats at race-adjacent intensity is well-supported by this data (150m-to-200m and
300m-to-200m correlations were among the higher entries in Table 42), more so than a
program relying mainly on much shorter (30m) segments for that specific event.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification these
correlated exercises fall into. [[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] —
the much weaker transfer picture for non-running assistance exercises in the same event
group.

# The Barbell Snatch and Half Squat Transfer to Sprinting Only Up to a Narrow, Specific Performance Band, Then Stop

**What it is** — Tables 51-60 (PDF pp. 91-99, printed pp. 74-82) correlate the barbell
snatch and half squat (with barbell on shoulders) against 100m/200m/400m and hurdle
results across five to six performance bands per event. Bondarchuk's own reading: overall
interrelationship is poor, and where a positive ("cumulative") effect exists at all, it is
confined to specific, narrow bands rather than holding across all qualification levels.
Examples with locators: men's 100m snatch/squat "cumulative effect" only up to
11.10-11.40s (Table 51: snatch coefficients range from -0.186 at 10.20-10.50s up to only
0.396 at 11.10-11.40s); women's snatch shows an effect on only one band, 12.70-12.79s
(Table 56); in the 400m hurdles, "a positive interrelationship... was not seen" at all,
with correlation coefficients ranging only 0.196-0.320 (Table 55 itself at PDF p. 95,
printed p. 78; the "not seen" summary sentence and the 0.196-0.320 range are Bondarchuk's
own text at PDF p. 89, printed p. 72). Throws of the shot forward/backward
were even weaker transfer exercises, positive only for 110m hurdlers at two narrow bands
(13.50-14.00s and 14.00-14.50s) and absent elsewhere. (PDF pp. 88-90, printed pp. 71-73.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: "the cumulative effect from strength
exercises will appear only when they are close to the competitive event according to the
biomechanical aspects and methodological parameters" (PDF p. 102, printed p. 85) — i.e.
the snatch and squat are specialized-preparatory (per
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]), sharing muscle groups with sprinting but
not its movement structure, velocity, or ground-contact regime, so per
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] they sit further from the competitive
event in the transfer chain than the running-based exercises in
[[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]]. He explicitly declines to
call this "ineffectiveness," instead suggesting the missing transfer could be a
methodological artifact (rep count, session compactness, intensity zones used) rather than
a fixed property of the exercises. (PDF p. 102, printed p. 85.)

**When to apply** — Use as historical caution against assuming barbell strength numbers
(snatch, squat) will keep predicting sprint improvement once an athlete passes a certain
performance level; per this data, once an athlete is already fast, further improvement in
these lifts stops tracking with further sprint improvement. This does not mean drop the
lifts (see [[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for
Bondarchuk's own prescription on that point) — it means stop expecting them to be the
driver of further sprint gains at that point.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite and sub-elite
Soviet-era sprinters/hurdlers, both sexes, tested with a specific barbell snatch and a
half-squat-with-barbell-on-shoulders (not a full back squat, front squat, or trap-bar
variant); the finding should not be assumed to hold for a different strength exercise
variation without its own data. This is track and field data; extending "barbell strength
work plateaus in its transfer to top-end speed past a certain level" to football speed
training is Inference. No outside source was checked in this ingest to confirm whether
this pattern holds beyond Bondarchuk's own dataset; treat it as this book's finding only
until cross-checked.

**Example** — A high-level 100m sprinter already running 10.2-10.4s should not expect
squat or snatch PRs to reliably predict further 100m improvement, per this data; a
developing sprinter in the 11.0-11.5s range is more likely to still be inside the band
where this book's data shows a measurable (if still modest) positive relationship.

**Related** — [[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]] — the much
stronger transfer picture for running-based assistance work in the same event group.
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] — Bondarchuk's own
prescription for what to do once an exercise stops producing further transfer.

# Among Assistance Exercises, Multi-Jump Work (Ten-Fold Jump, Leg-to-Leg Bounds) Transfers to Sprinting Most Consistently — More Than Single Jumps, Throws, or Barbell Lifts

**What it is** — Comparing all the specialized-preparatory assistance exercises tested
against sprint/hurdle competitive results (barbell snatch, half squat, standing long jump,
vertical jump, triple jump from place, 10-fold jump from place, leg-to-leg jumps for 50m,
forward/backward shot throws), Bondarchuk identifies the **10-fold jump from place** and
**leg-to-leg (bounding) jumps for 50m** as "more transferable than other specialized-
preparatory exercises," measured not by having the single highest correlation coefficient
but by the number of qualification-level bands across which a positive cumulative effect
appears (PDF p. 99, printed p. 82). Concretely: leg-to-leg jumps for 50m showed a
cumulative effect on **all levels** for both men's and women's 100m, and across the full
range for women's 100m hurdles (12.80-15.80s) and men's 400m hurdles (49.50-55.50s) (PDF
p. 100, printed p. 83). By contrast, the standing long jump, vertical jump, and triple
jump from place each showed positive transfer only on two-to-three of five levels for most
events, and high jump/pole vault-style single jumps were even more level-restricted for
sprint events specifically (not their own competitive event). He generalizes: "with an
increase in a number of take-offs when executing the above mentioned jump exercises, there
is an increase in the number of cases of positive transfer" — proposing multi-jump
exercises over long ground-contact segments (20-150m) as the most broadly transferable
jump category for track and field generally. (PDF pp. 100-101, printed pp. 83-84.)

**Why it works** — His own stated mechanism: multi-jump exercises over distance "repeat
the biomechanical parameters of the competitive movement" more closely than single jumps,
"have a similar appearance to the muscle work regimes, and use the same intensity zones,"
and can duplicate the sprint's actual duration/segment structure (e.g. matching a starting-
acceleration segment specifically). (PDF p. 101, printed p. 84.) In the terms of
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], repeated bounding over a real sprint-
relevant distance sits closer to specialized-developmental than a single standing jump
does, which under [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] predicts exactly
the stronger, more level-consistent transfer observed here.

**When to apply** — When choosing between plyometric/jump exercise variants for a
sprint-focused program, this data favors prioritizing repeated multi-jump/bounding work
over set distances (matched to the target phase of the sprint — acceleration vs. max
velocity) over single-effort jumps (standing long jump, vertical jump) as the more
consistently transferable choice, while still using single jumps for their own
diagnostic/training value.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
sprinters and hurdlers, both sexes; "leg-to-leg jumps for 50m" and "10-fold jump from
place" are specific, defined tests in this text, not a stand-in for every modern bounding
or plyometric variation. The claim is about *transfer consistency across qualification
levels*, not about which exercise has the single highest correlation value — do not
conflate the two when citing this entry. Applying this preference (multi-jump over
single-jump assistance work) to football speed/power training is Inference; no outside
plyometrics source was checked in this ingest to confirm the pattern holds beyond
Bondarchuk's own track and field dataset.

**Example** — A sprint-development block choosing between a session of standing long
jumps and a session of 10-15 continuous alternate-leg bounds over 30-50m would, per this
data, expect the bounding session to transfer more reliably across a wider range of athlete

# Throwing Lighter and Heavier Versions of the Same Implement Transfers to the Competitive Throw Almost Universally, Across Nearly Every Level of Mastery

**What it is** — Tables 69-84 (PDF pp. 116-130, printed pp. 99-113) correlate results
throwing lighter/heavier implement weights (e.g., a 5-10kg shot, a 1.5-2.5kg discus, a
0.5-1kg javelin, a 3-16kg hammer/weight) against the competitive-weight throw, for men and
women across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer. Bondarchuk's summary: "there is
almost always a place for mutually correlated interrelationships... the amounts of these
interrelationships are sufficiently great," with only two exceptions found in the entire
dataset (javelin: no relationship between the 0.6kg implement and the 3-4kg standing
throw; no relationship between the 0.7kg and 4kg implements). (PDF p. 132, printed p.
115.) He illustrates the practical power of this with individual elite-athlete case data
(**single-case, untested**, not aggregate correlation): two-time Olympic hammer champion
Yu. Sedikh held unofficial world-best-adjacent marks in the 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10kg
implements and the 16kg weight alongside his 86.74m competitive record, with year-by-year
dynamics (1980-86) showing his lighter/heavier implement results moving in lockstep with
his competitive result in 35 of 38 tracked instances (Tables 85-86, PDF pp. 130-131,
printed pp. 113-114). Discus thrower R. Ubartasa's five-year log similarly shows his
implement-weight throws increasing alongside his competitive result in 29 of 34 instances
(Table 88, PDF p. 141, printed p. 124).

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: lighter/heavier-implement throws are
"identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the
muscular groups... the muscle work regimes and so on" (PDF p. 98, printed p. 115) — in
the terms of [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], this is as close to a pure
specialized-developmental exercise as exists in this book (the same movement, only the
resistance changes), which under [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]]
predicts exactly the near-universal positive transfer observed.

**When to apply** — This is the strongest, most consistent transfer finding in the entire
book: for throwing events specifically, varying implement weight while keeping the
competitive movement intact is a reliably transferable training method across nearly the
full range of athlete qualification, more consistent than any strength, jump, or sprint
assistance exercise tested elsewhere in this chapter. He does flag a real caveat: heavier
implements can degrade technique (release angle, trunk lean, reduced amplitude), an effect
he says clears up "in several weekly cycles" once the heavier implement is dropped — the
double-effect pattern named in [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]].

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported for the aggregate correlational
finding (Tables 69-84)**, but the Sedikh/Ubartasa/Shulta individual case data (Tables
85-88) is **untested**: single elite-athlete case studies, presented as illustration, not
as independent evidence of the mechanism, and Bondarchuk himself frames them as examples
rather than proof. Population throughout is elite Soviet-bloc throwers (Olympic and world
champions/record holders for the case studies). This finding is specific to implements
that can be made lighter or heavier while keeping the throwing motion otherwise intact
(shot, discus, javelin, hammer); there is no directly equivalent implement-weight
manipulation in most football skills, so applying "vary the resistance, keep the movement
identical" as a general training principle to football (e.g., weighted-ball throwing for a
quarterback) is Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.

**Example** — A hammer thrower's training plan built around a rotation of 5-6 different
implement weights (lighter and heavier than competition weight) targeting both speed and
strength qualities within the same movement pattern is strongly supported by this data as
a transfer-reliable method, more so than substituting generic barbell strength work for
that same purpose (see [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]).

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining this exercise's near-maximal transfer. [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]
— the much more limited transfer picture for barbell strength exercises in the same event
group. [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]] — the double-effect pattern behind the
heavier-implement technique caveat.

 "}, {"page": 2, "viewer_page": 3, "text": "About the Author 
 
Anatoliy Bondarchuk 
 
Dr. Anatoly Bondarchuk is renowned as an athlete (1972 Olympic Champion and 
European Champion in the hammer throw as well as a former World Record Holder) and 
Mr. Bondarchuk's coaching credentials are virtually unprecedented in the sport of 
Athletics.  
 
Dr. Bondarchuk is a Doctor of Pedagogical Science (University of Kiev ) and his 
research into technique and high-performance training methods formed the basis for 
many of the common techniques and practices used by the world's top athletes today. Mr. 
Bondarchuk developed the USSR National Team throws program from 1976 to 1992 
from which he produced numerous World and Olympic Champions in the Hammer, 
Discus and Shot Put. He has authored 11 books and 195 articles in his areas of expertise. 
A common focus is training to maintain performance and technique. Since 1992 he has 
been coaching for Portugal and Kuwait.  
 
Mr. Bondarchuk's athletes, while members of the USSR National Team, broke 12 World 
Records, and still hold the current world record in the hammer throw. His athletes won all 
hammer throw medals in 4 consecutive non-boycotted Olympic Games. 
i "}, {"page": 3, "viewer_page": 4, "text": "About the Translator 
 
Dr. Michael Yessis 
 
Dr. Michael Yessis received his Ph.D. from the University of Southern California and his 
B.S. and M.S. from City University of New York. He is president of Sports Training, 
Inc., a diverse sports and fitness company. Dr. Yessis is also Professor Emeritus at 
California State University, Fullerton, where he is a multi-sports specialist in 
biomechanics (technique analysis) and sports conditioning and training.  
 
In his work, Dr. Yessis has developed many unique specialized strength and speed-
strength (explosive) training programs. He has served as training and technique 
consultant to several Olympic and professional sports teams, including the L.A. Rams 
and L.A. Raiders football clubs, Natadore Diving Team, and the U.S. Men's Volleyball 
Team. He has also successfully trained many athletes in different sports.  
 
Dr. Yessis has written 16 books including Kinesiology of Exercise, Explosive Running, 
Build A Better Athlete, and Sports: Is It All B.S.?    He has also written more than 2,000 
articles on fitness and sports training that have appeared in magazines such as Muscle and 
Fitness, Shape, Scholastic Coach, Fitness Management, and the National Strength and 
Conditioning Association Journal. In addition, he has completed four videos;  Exercise 
Mastery, Developing a Quarterback's Arm and Strength, Specialized Strength and 
Explosive Exercises for Baseball and Specialized Strength and Explosive Exercises for 
Softball. 
 
 
 
ii "}]

`{"pages": 236, "text_pages": 216, "scanned": false}`), not scanned. A second copy of

scan and was **not** used for this ingest; ignore it for any future batch on this title.

**Print-to-PDF page offset.** Two regimes:
- **Front matter (roman numerals i-xvi):** PDF page = roman position + 1 (PDF p.2 =

- **Main body (arabic, Chapter 1 onward): PDF page = printed page + 17.** Verified at
  three independent chapter starts, not just the offset's origin point: Chapter 1
  (printed p.1 = PDF p.18, "A Brief Overview of Training Transfer"), Chapter 2 (printed

  offset holds unchanged from PDF p.18 through at least PDF p.215 (printed p.198, end of
  Chapter 3's "Conclusions"); no evidence of a mid-book repagination.

**Confidence rule for this book (per `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md`):** the whole book is a
single author's own research program (his stated corpus: "more than 7,000 athletes"
tested by questionnaire and correlational analysis over roughly two decades, entirely
within the USSR system he coached, no independent replication cited in the excerpted
chapters). Per the brief's rule for Soviet-era/single-lab findings, everything ingested
from this book is capped at `supported`, and dropped to `untested` for the author's own
single, unverified theoretical proposals (e.g. the "three situations" transfer-timing
model) or single-case illustrations (e.g. the A-B-C tie-in-effect example, individual
elite-athlete case tables). Nothing in the excerpted chapters rises to `proven` in this
batch: even where a concept (e.g. positive/negative/neutral transfer) echoes a name
Bondarchuk himself cites from outside his own study (Thorndike), no outside source was
independently checked in this ingest, so every entry stays capped `supported` or lower and
says explicitly, in its own words, when a broader claim is this entry's own reading rather
than something either Bondarchuk or a checked citation states.

Every reported correlation coefficient in this book is presented **without sample sizes,
significance tests, or population age/sex breakdowns beyond "high qualification" vs "low
qualification"** groups (the tables' own note: "the coefficient of correlation of high
level athletes is in the numerator and for low level athletes, in the denominator," with
the numerator/denominator convention flipped without warning between the sprint tables
(41-50, high/low) and the throws tables (70, 72, 74, 76, 78: "low qualifications... in the
numerator and high level athletes in the denominator" — the reverse). This flip is real,
not a transcription slip; see `claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations.md`
and `claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal.md` for the locators. Treat
any single number pulled from these tables with that reversal risk in mind.

The population throughout is **elite and sub-elite USSR-system track and field athletes**
(sprinters, hurdlers, jumpers, throwers, middle/long/ultra-distance runners, race
walkers), tested during Bondarchuk's tenure with the USSR national throws program
(1976-92) and cited co-authors' data. **Nothing here is football, team-sport, or
non-track-and-field population data.** Any application to football or other team sports
in these entries' "When to apply" sections is explicitly marked Inference.

# The Book's Four Exercise Classes, from Its Own Glossary: General Preparatory, Specialized-Preparatory, Specialized-Developmental, Competitive

**What it is** — This is the book's own definition of the classification Chapter 2's
correlational data depends on, drawn from its front-matter Glossary (PDF pp. 10-14,
printed pp. ix-xiii; Chapter 2's own prose, PDF p. 75, printed p. 58, assumes the reader
already knows these terms and does not redefine them). **Voice note:** the book credits
"About the Author" (Bondarchuk) and "About the Translator" (Michael Yessis) separately,
and the Glossary itself carries no byline. Definitions inside it cite the book's own
numbered bibliography (e.g. the "Block method" entry cites "Y.V. Verkhoshansky [49, 50]"
using the same reference numbers Bondarchuk's own chapters use), which is evidence the
Glossary is Bondarchuk's own material carried through translation rather than a
translator's separate addition — but the book gives no explicit statement either way, so
this entry treats the Glossary as **the book's** definitions rather than asserting they are
Bondarchuk's personal wording. Do not cite this entry as "Bondarchuk says" in a future
entry without that caveat:
- **General (Preparatory) Exercises / GPP**: "do not repeat the competitive actions as a
  whole or their separate parts. Other muscle groups take part in the work being done. The
  functional systems of the body are activated but do not ensure an increase in results in
  the competitive exercise." Function: all-round development, work capacity, and active
  rest/restoration. (PDF p. 12, printed p. x.)
- **Specialized-Preparatory Exercises / SPP**: like general exercises, "do not repeat the
  competitive actions as a whole or in their separate parts. However, they use similar
  muscle groups in their execution," activating the functions and body systems the main
  movement depends on, with "identical or close to identical regimes of muscle work."
  (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Specialized-Developmental Exercises / SDE**: "repeat the competitive exercise in its
  separate parts. In executing them, one and the same muscle groups participate, together
  with activation of similar systems and organs. They not only repeat the muscle work
  regime and other systems of the body... but also supersede them," and "serve for entry
  into the state of sports form." (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Competitive Exercises / CE**: "the acting definition... is 'sport event,' in which the
  athlete participates in competition," executed either in actual competition or in
  training as a model/repeat of competitive conditions, easier or harder. (PDF p. 12,
  printed p. x-xi.)
Chapter 2's own intro adds a cross-cutting distinction independent of the four classes: a
**local** exercise (uses separate parts/body links — squat, bench press, standing long
jump, vertical jump) versus a **global** exercise (uses all body links together — the
barbell clean). (PDF p. 75, printed p. 58.)

**Why it works** — The Glossary gives no stated mechanism for why these four classes
should differ in transfer value; it only defines them by how much of the competitive
movement each one reproduces. **Inference:** reading the four classes as an ordered
continuum, and connecting that continuum to
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and the specifist "identical
elements" position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] (more shared
elements with the competitive movement predicting more reliable transfer), is this entry's
own synthesis across sections of the book, not a claim the Glossary or Chapter 2's intro
states in those words. Chapter 2's correlational data (see the claim entries below) can be
read as an empirical test of that inferred prediction, event by event, but the book itself
does not frame its own tables that way.

**When to apply** — Use as the primary-source definition when auditing any exercise
selection against this taxonomy, in place of or alongside secondary paraphrases of it.
**Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in HHPR 5355 is taught "on a spectrum from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of 'sport specific'"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`; `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`) — this entry
gives that course material its primary-source citation and exact definitions. This
library already has a secondary-source treatment of the same taxonomy in
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault), built from Moyer's course paraphrase rather than Bondarchuk's own text; that
entry's table ("GPE/SPE/SDE/CE") matches this one closely but labels Moyer's own sprint
examples (bounding, banded pawback, etc.), not Bondarchuk's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, not proven: this is Bondarchuk's own
classification scheme. Two other sources in this library already use it independently
(the `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer` vault entry linked above, and Eric's HHPR 5355
course per `method-baseline.md`), which is evidence the taxonomy circulated beyond this
one book, but this ingest did not check how far it spread through the wider Soviet/Russian
sport-science literature, so that broader claim is not made here. It is a practitioner
taxonomy, not an independently tested causal model, and the boundary between
classes is fuzzy in application (the Moyer-derived entry below makes the same point about
sprint exercises specifically). The four-class definitions here are written for individual
track and field events; a football skill (e.g., a pass rush) is a much less discrete,
single "competitive exercise" than a 100m sprint or a hammer throw, so classifying a given
drill as SPP vs. SDE for football is Inference, not something Bondarchuk's glossary
addresses.

**Example** — For a shot putter: general preparatory = general conditioning running;
specialized-preparatory = barbell snatch, half squat (same leg-extensor muscle groups,
different movement); specialized-developmental = throwing a lighter or heavier shot

# Bondarchuk Publishes 34 Normative Tables Linking Assistance-Exercise Results to Competitive-Result Bands, by Age and Qualification

**What it is** — Tables 1-34 (PDF pp. 44-67, printed pp. 27-50; this ingest sampled
representative tables rather than transcribing all 34) give normative "model
characteristics": for a given competitive-result band (e.g., 100m in 10.00-10.20s vs.
10.80-11.00s), a matching range of expected results in assistance exercises. Examples
pulled directly: **Table 1** ties 100m sprint splits (10m through 100m segments) to
five 100m-time bands. **Table 2** ties speed-strength markers (standing long jump,
triple/5-fold/10-fold jump from place, single-leg and alternate-leg jumps for time) to
those same five 100m bands — e.g., a 10.00-10.20s sprinter should stand-long-jump
3.10-3.30m, a 10.80-11.00s sprinter 2.70-2.90m. Similar tables exist for 200m, 400m,
women's 100m hurdles, and age-banded (15-16 / 17-18 / 19+) versions for 400m men and
women across successive preparatory/competitive periods (Tables 10-14). Table 8 also
gives named-athlete individual data (L. Evans, T. Smith, V. Markin, and others) tying
100m/200m/repeated-200m splits to final 400m results and a derived "speed reserve"
metric (400m result minus the doubled 200m split, e.g. L. Evans: 0.765s reserve).
(PDF pp. 44-51, printed pp. 27-34.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given; these are purely descriptive normative
benchmarks compiled from the author's dataset, presented as targets an athlete "should"
hit at a given competitive level, not as evidence of a causal relationship. **Inference:**
this functions the same way modern S&C "standards tables" (e.g., a vertical-jump-by-40-
time chart) function — useful as a rough talent-identification or gap-analysis tool, not
as proof that improving the assistance-exercise number will improve the competitive time.

**When to apply** — Use as a historical reference point or sanity check when building
Baylor's own sport-specific normative tables (a named gap in `method-baseline.md`,
"Testing and assessment," citing `performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase
2`): Bondarchuk's tables show what a rigorous, qualification-banded normative table looks
like (multiple assistance exercises per competitive-result band, banded by age where
relevant), even though the specific numbers are 1970s-80s Soviet track and field data and
not directly usable for a 2026 football roster.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, and only as a description that these
tables exist and roughly what they show — this entry does not treat any individual number
as validated for use as a current standard. The population is elite/sub-elite Soviet-era
male and female track and field athletes (refs [52], [74], [75] per the tables), not
football players; the specific split times, jump distances, and the Table 8 "speed
reserve" formula are Inference if applied to any other sport or era without
re-derivation. This ingest did not transcribe all 34 tables (only Tables 1-14 were pulled
in full); a future batch revisiting this chapter should note that gap before citing a
table number 15-34 that was not directly checked here.

**Example** — A recruiting or testing-standards project comparing "where does our sprinter
sit" could borrow the *format* (competitive-result band -> matching assistance-exercise
range, split by age where useful) from Table 2/10-14 without adopting the actual Soviet-
era numbers.

**Related** — No existing library entry covers normative benchmark tables directly; see
Eric's own gap analysis in `method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," for the live
Baylor need this table format could inform.

# Jump-from-a-Short-Run-Up Is the Single Most Transferable Assistance Exercise for Every Jump Event; High Jump Is the Outlier

**What it is** — Tables 61-68 (PDF pp. 104-112, printed pp. 87-95) correlate running,
jumping, and strength/throw exercises against long jump, high jump, triple jump, and pole
vault results, men and women. Across long jump, triple jump, and pole vault, **all**
running and jumping exercises showed a cumulative positive effect; the two throwing
exercises (shot forward/backward) showed essentially none. The single strongest, most
consistent exercise across event types was the **jump/vault with a short run-up**: long
jumpers' correlation to a short-approach jump ran 0.721-0.890 for men, 0.830-0.967 for
women (Tables 61-62); triple jumpers' short-run-up triple jump ran 0.890-0.954 for men,
0.700-0.906 for women (Tables 65-66); pole vaulters' short-run-up vault ran 0.706-0.845
for men, 0.788-0.865 for women (Tables 67-68). **High
jump was the outlier**: the author states plainly that in men's and women's high jump,
"in all cases, a weak interrelationship between the test results was observed on the
0.400 level" for running exercises specifically. Instead, per his prose (PDF p. 105,
printed p. 88), "the most informative and transferable exercise appears to be the vertical
jump with a short run-up," at 0.876-0.945 (men) / 0.865-0.965 (women) — **note an
unresolved source discrepancy**: those exact figures match the "10-fold jump from place"
row in Tables 63-64 (men 0.876-0.945, women 0.886-0.965), not the row literally labeled
"Jump from a short run-up" in the same tables (men 0.706-0.805, women 0.680-0.808, which
the prose separately describes as merely "sufficiently high"). This may be a
translation/editing inconsistency between the prose's exercise name and the table's row
label; do not assume which one is authoritative without checking the original Russian or
a second translation. Barbell snatch showed almost no
transfer anywhere in this section except isolated single-level effects; the half squat
with barbell transferred more consistently, especially for high jump and pole vault (all
levels for both sexes in those two events). (PDF pp. 104-113, printed pp. 87-96.)

**Why it works** — Per [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] and
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]], the short-run-up version of each
event's own competitive movement is itself a specialized-developmental exercise (repeats
the competitive action's parts under an altered, easier condition), so it sits closest to
the competitive event in the transfer chain — consistent with it outperforming
general-preparatory sprint and strength exercises across every jump event tested. High
jump's break from the sprint-correlated pattern of the other three jump events is not
explained mechanistically by the author; **Inference:** the high jump's approach and
takeoff (curved run, back-to-the-bar rotation) differs enough biomechanically from a
straight-line sprint that raw straight-ahead sprint speed may simply share fewer
"identical elements" with it than with long jump, triple jump, or pole vault approaches.

**When to apply** — When selecting assistance work for a jump-event athlete, this data
supports prioritizing a short-approach version of the competitive jump itself as the
highest-value transfer exercise, over generic sprint times or barbell strength numbers,
with the explicit exception of high jump, where multi-jump (10-fold) and short-approach
vertical jump work outperformed straight sprint speed as a predictor.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
long jumpers, high jumpers, triple jumpers, and pole vaulters, both sexes. The "high jump
breaks the pattern" finding is specific to Bondarchuk's Soviet-era high jump technique
population (likely predominantly the Fosbury Flop or straddle technique of that era) and
should not be over-generalized without checking which technique his athletes used (not
stated in the excerpted pages). Applying any of these specific exercise priorities to a
football skill (e.g., a receiver's high-point jump) is Inference — no football population
data exists in this source.

**Example** — A long jump program prioritizing short-approach full-technique jumps (at
reduced run-up length) as the top assistance tool, alongside sprint work, is
well-supported by this data; the same prioritization for a high jumper should shift toward
short-approach vertical jumps and multi-jump work rather than assuming sprint speed
transfers the same way.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining why the short-run-up version outperforms more general exercises.
[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]] — the parallel finding for
sprinters using jump exercises as assistance work (the reverse direction of transfer).

14	# The Book's Four Exercise Classes, from Its Own Glossary: General Preparatory, Specialized-Preparatory, Specialized-Developmental, Competitive
15	
16	**What it is** — This is the book's own definition of the classification Chapter 2's
17	correlational data depends on, drawn from its front-matter Glossary (PDF pp. 10-14,
18	printed pp. ix-xiii; Chapter 2's own prose, PDF p. 75, printed p. 58, assumes the reader
19	already knows these terms and does not redefine them). **Voice note:** the book credits
20	"About the Author" (Bondarchuk) and "About the Translator" (Michael Yessis) separately,
21	and the Glossary itself carries no byline. Definitions inside it cite the book's own
22	numbered bibliography (e.g. the "Block method" entry cites "Y.V. Verkhoshansky [49, 50]"
23	using the same reference numbers Bondarchuk's own chapters use), which is evidence the
24	Glossary is Bondarchuk's own material carried through translation rather than a
25	translator's separate addition — but the book gives no explicit statement either way, so
26	this entry treats the Glossary as **the book's** definitions rather than asserting they are
27	Bondarchuk's personal wording. Do not cite this entry as "Bondarchuk says" in a future
28	entry without that caveat:
29	- **General (Preparatory) Exercises / GPP**: "do not repeat the competitive actions as a
30	  whole or their separate parts. Other muscle groups take part in the work being done. The
31	  functional systems of the body are activated but do not ensure an increase in results in
32	  the competitive exercise." Function: all-round development, work capacity, and active
33	  rest/restoration. (PDF p. 12, printed p. xi.)
34	- **Specialized-Preparatory Exercises / SPP**: like general exercises, "do not repeat the
35	  competitive actions as a whole or in their separate parts. However, they use similar
36	  muscle groups in their execution," activating the functions and body systems the main
37	  movement depends on, with "identical or close to identical regimes of muscle work."
38	  (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
39	- **Specialized-Developmental Exercises / SDE**: "repeat the competitive exercise in its
40	  separate parts. In executing them, one and the same muscle groups participate, together
41	  with activation of similar systems and organs. They not only repeat the muscle work
42	  regime and other systems of the body... but also supersede them," and "serve for entry
43	  into the state of sports form." (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
44	- **Competitive Exercises / CE**: "the acting definition... is 'sport event,' in which the
45	  athlete participates in competition," executed either in actual competition or in
46	  training as a model/repeat of competitive conditions, easier or harder (this definition
47	  spans a page break). (PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. x-xi.)
48	Chapter 2's own intro adds a cross-cutting distinction independent of the four classes: a

# The Book's Four Exercise Classes, from Its Own Glossary: General Preparatory, Specialized-Preparatory, Specialized-Developmental, Competitive

**What it is** — This is the book's own definition of the classification Chapter 2's
correlational data depends on, drawn from its front-matter Glossary (PDF pp. 10-14,
printed pp. ix-xiii; Chapter 2's own prose, PDF p. 75, printed p. 58, assumes the reader
already knows these terms and does not redefine them). **Voice note:** the book credits
"About the Author" (Bondarchuk) and "About the Translator" (Michael Yessis) separately,
and the Glossary itself carries no byline. Definitions inside it cite the book's own
numbered bibliography (e.g. the "Block method" entry cites "Y.V. Verkhoshansky [49, 50]"
using the same reference numbers Bondarchuk's own chapters use), which is evidence the
Glossary is Bondarchuk's own material carried through translation rather than a
translator's separate addition — but the book gives no explicit statement either way, so
this entry treats the Glossary as **the book's** definitions rather than asserting they are
Bondarchuk's personal wording. Do not cite this entry as "Bondarchuk says" in a future
entry without that caveat:
- **General (Preparatory) Exercises / GPP**: "do not repeat the competitive actions as a
  whole or their separate parts. Other muscle groups take part in the work being done. The
  functional systems of the body are activated but do not ensure an increase in results in
  the competitive exercise." Function: all-round development, work capacity, and active
  rest/restoration. (PDF p. 12, printed p. xi.)
- **Specialized-Preparatory Exercises / SPP**: like general exercises, "do not repeat the
  competitive actions as a whole or in their separate parts. However, they use similar
  muscle groups in their execution," activating the functions and body systems the main
  movement depends on, with "identical or close to identical regimes of muscle work."
  (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Specialized-Developmental Exercises / SDE**: "repeat the competitive exercise in its
  separate parts. In executing them, one and the same muscle groups participate, together
  with activation of similar systems and organs. They not only repeat the muscle work
  regime and other systems of the body... but also supersede them," and "serve for entry
  into the state of sports form." (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Competitive Exercises / CE**: "the acting definition... is 'sport event,' in which the
  athlete participates in competition," executed either in actual competition or in
  training as a model/repeat of competitive conditions, easier or harder (this definition
  spans a page break). (PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. x-xi.)
Chapter 2's own intro adds a cross-cutting distinction independent of the four classes: a
**local** exercise (uses separate parts/body links — squat, bench press, standing long
jump, vertical jump) versus a **global** exercise (uses all body links together — the
barbell clean). (PDF p. 75, printed p. 58.)

**Why it works** — The Glossary gives no stated mechanism for why these four classes
should differ in transfer value; it only defines them by how much of the competitive
movement each one reproduces. **Inference:** reading the four classes as an ordered
continuum, and connecting that continuum to
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and the specifist "identical
elements" position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] (more shared
elements with the competitive movement predicting more reliable transfer), is this entry's
own synthesis across sections of the book, not a claim the Glossary or Chapter 2's intro
states in those words. Chapter 2's correlational data (see the claim entries below) can be
read as an empirical test of that inferred prediction, event by event, but the book itself
does not frame its own tables that way.

**When to apply** — Use as the primary-source definition when auditing any exercise
selection against this taxonomy, in place of or alongside secondary paraphrases of it.
**Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in HHPR 5355 is taught "on a spectrum from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of 'sport specific'"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`; `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`) — this entry
gives that course material its primary-source citation and exact definitions. This
library already has a secondary-source treatment of the same taxonomy in
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault), built from Moyer's course paraphrase rather than Bondarchuk's own text; that
entry's table ("GPE/SPE/SDE/CE") matches this one closely but labels Moyer's own sprint
examples (bounding, banded pawback, etc.), not Bondarchuk's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, not proven: this is Bondarchuk's own
classification scheme. Two other sources in this library already use it independently
(the `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer` vault entry linked above, and Eric's HHPR 5355
course per `method-baseline.md`), which is evidence the taxonomy circulated beyond this
one book, but this ingest did not check how far it spread through the wider Soviet/Russian
sport-science literature, so that broader claim is not made here. It is a practitioner
taxonomy, not an independently tested causal model, and the boundary between
classes is fuzzy in application (the Moyer-derived entry below makes the same point about
sprint exercises specifically). The four-class definitions here are written for individual
track and field events; a football skill (e.g., a pass rush) is a much less discrete,
single "competitive exercise" than a 100m sprint or a hammer throw, so classifying a given
drill as SPP vs. SDE for football is Inference, not something Bondarchuk's glossary
addresses.

**Example** — For a shot putter: general preparatory = general conditioning running;
specialized-preparatory = barbell snatch, half squat (same leg-extensor muscle groups,
different movement); specialized-developmental = throwing a lighter or heavier shot
(repeats the throw's parts under altered load); competitive = throwing the 7.26kg
competition shot in a meet.

**Related** — `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault) — the secondary, Moyer-course paraphrase of this same taxonomy; **reciprocal-link
suggestion**: add a note there pointing back to this primary-source entry once this book
clears the review gate. [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — the transfer
logic built on this classification. [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] —
the specifist theory this classification operationalizes.
